Background: Violence against women (VAW) and violence against children (VAC) carry profound physical, emotional, and economic consequences. Yet the full economic burden has not been comprehensively characterised. This study assesses the economic burden of VAC and VAW in Canada.

Methods: We conducted a multi-method, population-based economic assessment for children under 15 and women 15-75 years, guided by an adapted costing framework. Costing captured individual, public system, and macroeconomic perspectives over annual and lifetime horizons, using the 2018 Survey on Safety in Public and Private Spaces and administrative data. Analyses incorporated healthcare utilisation, productivity losses, labour market impacts, attributable health outcomes. Costs are in 2024 Canadian dollars.

Findings: The annual economic burden of VAC was $51.2 billion ($31.7-$57.6 billion), driven by future earnings losses ($43.2 billion) and child protection expenditures ($8.0 billion). For VAW, the annual burden was $6.2 billion ($4.5-$7.4 billion), borne by individuals ($4.5 billion) and by public systems ($1.7 billion) and macroeconomic losses reached $0.6 billion. Lifetime health-related costs (VAC: $22.6 billion; VAW: $25.2 billion) were dominated by mental health conditions.

Interpretation: This is the first integrated Canadian estimate of the economic burden of VAC and VAW, demonstrating that violence is a public health and economic crisis. Findings support urgent investment in prevention, early intervention, trauma-informed care, and cross-sectoral policy responses. Our framework is transferable for monitoring progress and evaluating policy reform.

detail.abstract: Corporate hierarchies rarely reconfigure themselves overnight, yet the Chief Information Officer role has undergone precisely that kind of abrupt structural upheaval. Four independent industry surveys conducted between late 2024 and early 2026 (Foundry/CIO.com, n=1,156; Deloitte, n=622; Gartner, n=3,186; McKinsey, n=632) converge on a striking portrait: 65% of CIOs now report directly to the CEO, 36% carry profit-and-loss accountability, and 80% spearhead enterprise AI evaluation. Grounding these practitioner findings in upper echelons theory, strategic alignment theory, and established IT governance frameworks, this paper documents the metamorphosis and contends that governing autonomous AI agents constitutes the CIO's most consequential emerging obligation. We scrutinize the security vulnerabilities that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) introduces into enterprise architectures, marshaling evidence that 80% of organizations have encountered hazardous AI agent behaviors and that 41.7% of audited MCP deployments harbor exploitable weaknesses. We then propose ContextGuard, a zero-trust governance architecture purpose-built for AI context protocol security, and advance three falsifiable research propositions linking CIO strategic positioning, zerotrust governance maturity, and organizational AI value realization.

detail.abstract: This essay argues that the concept of enclosure—the conversion of shared commons into private property—provides the most analytically precise frame for understanding a series of structural transformations that are typically treated as separate phenomena: the British parliamentary enclosures of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the Irish plantation system and its famine consequences, the Campanian masseria system and southern Italian emigration, the corporate capture of the internet commons, the enclosure of human creative and intellectual output in proprietary AI training data, and the emerging contest over renewable energy infrastructure. Drawing on the theoretical frameworks of E.P. Thompson, Karl Polanyi, Amartya Sen, Shoshana Zuboff, and Peter Linebaugh, and grounded in the author’s direct engagement with the landscapes of Ireland, Campania, and rural Massachusetts, the essay contends that enclosure is not a historical episode but a recurrent structural mechanism through which capital creates the conditions for accumulation by destroying the commons that previously sustained communities. The essay concludes by locating the care economy—the irreducibly relational work of sustaining human life across generations—as both the ultimate target of extractive enclosure and the most durable site of resistance to it.

detail.abstract: Indian higher-education institutions routinely set ranking ambitions — "top 50 in three years," "break into the top 100" — that assume a fluidity the data does not support. Using a six-year panel of ranked institutions across twelve NIRF disciplines (2020–2025; 3,282 year-over-year transitions), this paper characterises the actual dynamics of rank movement. It documents a pronounced mobility ceiling: 62% of institutions move five positions or fewer in a year, 81% move ten or fewer, and only 3.0% move more than 25 positions. Beneath this lies steep score compression — the total-score gap between adjacent ranks is roughly thirteen times larger at the top of a list than near the bottom — so the marginal effort to advance one place rises sharply with rank. Apparent cross-discipline volatility inverts depending on measurement: the deepest lists look most turbulent by raw positions, but the smallest disciplines are most volatile once cohort size is accounted for. Year-over-year movement is multifactorial, tracking faculty-capacity indicators most strongly in professional and teaching-led disciplines and research-output indicators most strongly in research-led ones, with no single indicator dominant. Movement into and out of the ranked lists is shown to be driven largely by administrative resizing of those lists rather than by competitive displacement. The findings reframe institutional strategy: advancement rewards precision over volume of effort, and the binding constraints on movement are structural.

title: From Financial Access to Financial Resilience: The Behavioral Financial Inclusion Gap
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Financial Access to Financial Resilience: The Behavioral Financial Inclusion Gap
detail.abstract: Formal access to financial services does not always translate into practices that strengthen resilience under economic stress. This paper investigates whether this disconnect is associated with weaker financial resilience by introducing the Behavioral Financial Inclusion Gap (BFIG), defined as the discrepancy between formal access and effective financial behavior. Using worldwide individual-level Global Findex microdata, we construct a score-based BFIG and an MCA-based alternative for robustness. We then examine its association with three complementary dimensions of resilience: the ability to sustain household expenses after an income shock, the use of savings as the main emergency coping mechanism, and the capacity to mobilize emergency funds from any substantive source. The empirical strategy combines binary logit models with a predictive extension using regularized logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost to assess whether the relationship remains stable under more flexible specifications. Across all models, evidence reveals a consistent pattern: a wider BFIG is associated with weaker resilience. The relationship is strongest for savings-based coping and coping capacity, indicating that incomplete behavioral inclusion affects not only whether households can respond to shocks, but also the quality and breadth of the resources they can mobilize. The predictive results reinforce this conclusion by showing that the BFIG remains relevant along with broader socioeconomic and digital-access characteristics. In general, the findings suggest that financial inclusion should be judged not only by formal access, but also by the degree to which that access is translated into effective financial behavior that improves resilience.

title: Europe Needs a Strategy to Close the Artificial Intelligence Compute Gap
affiliations: Bruegel and Tilburg Law and Economics Center (TILEC)

detail.title: Europe Needs a Strategy to Close the Artificial Intelligence Compute Gap
detail.abstract: The race to dominate artificial intelligence is to a large extent a race for compute, or processing power. Advanced AI systems require vast quantities of specialised chips able to run the calculations that train and operate large models. Whoever controls that infrastructure shapes the technology and sets the economic and strategic terms on which others access it.

title: Child Labor and Forced Work in the Cocoa Agroindustrial Supply Chain:: Certification Gaps, Traceability Deficits, and the Strategic Role of the United States in Building Ethical Sourcing Standards
affiliations: Universidad ECOTEC (Ecuador)

detail.title: Child Labor and Forced Work in the Cocoa Agroindustrial Supply Chain:: Certification Gaps, Traceability Deficits, and the Strategic Role of the United States in Building Ethical Sourcing Standards
detail.abstract: The global cocoa supply chain, which underlies a USD 130 billion chocolate industry, remains structurally exposed to child labor and forced labor, particularly in West African producing regions that account for approximately 70% of world cocoa output. Despite decades of voluntary industry commitments and the proliferation of third-party certification schemes-including Fairtrade, Rainforest Alliance, and UTZ-independent audits and investigative reports consistently document persistent labor violations affecting an estimated 1.56 million children in cocoa farming households in Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire alone (U.S. Department of Labor, 2022). This paper argues that existing certification frameworks suffer from three systemic deficiencies: (1) limited farmlevel traceability due to fragmented smallholder structures; (2) auditability gaps arising from multi-tier supply chains with opaque intermediary networks; and (3) insufficient integration with mandatory regulatory frameworks at the import level. Against this background, the United States Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA, 2021) and the broader HRDD (Human Rights Due Diligence) regulatory trend signal an imminent shift toward enforceable traceability requirements. This paper proposes an integrated model combining digital traceability technologies, farm-level registration systems, and policy-aligned certification standards as a viable pathway to close the current governance gap. The author draws on 18 years of direct operational experience in cocoa agroindustrial supply chains, logistics systems, and international trade compliance to identify actionable interventions that are technically feasible, economically viable, and strategically aligned with U.S. import policy objectives.

detail.abstract: Energy transition economics asks whether credible climate policy can reduce petroleum dependence before regulations become legally binding. This paper examines anticipatory responses to California's Advanced Clean Cars II (ACC II) regulation, adopted across 14 U.S. states during 2022-2023, with binding requirements beginning only in model years 2026-2027. Using a staggered difference-indifferences design on a balanced panel of 51 states from 2016 to 2023, we find no significant average anticipatory effect on electric vehicle adoption overall. However, later-adopting states exhibit a 3.9% increase in electric vehicle stock, consistent with a policy credibility mechanism. We calibrate the estimated policy effects into a GTAP-E-Power framework to evaluate global welfare and energy-security implications. Credible electric vehicle mandates reduce petroleum dependence and redistribute welfare primarily through terms-of-trade adjustments, operating through the same transmission channels as major oil supply disruptions, but in the opposite direction. The findings have direct implications for energy security policy in petroleum-importing economies seeking to reduce geopolitical exposure to global fossil fuel supply chains.

detail.abstract: Pakistan's LLB is the only degree in the country's higher education system whose content is inherently, irreversibly national, built entirely from Pakistan's own Constitution, statutes, jurisprudence, and legal framework. Yet Pakistan currently accepts a foreign law degree, specifically the University of London's Graduate Entry LLB teaching English law, for professional legal practice, while offering no equivalent domestic graduate entry pathway for its own most qualified professional graduates. This proposal presents a research-based, data-supported, institutionally grounded case for the introduction of a Graduate Entry LLB through Open and Distance Learning, designed for holders of recognized professional bachelor's degrees, deliverable through existing national infrastructure, and priced at a rate proportionally fair to Pakistan's income level. It requires no new institutions, no new legislation, and no new public expenditure. It requires one policy decision.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the factors associated with niyyah (worshipful intention) of Islamic bankers toward issuing green sukuk (G-sukuk) investment instruments. In particular, it analyses how bankers' empathy, moral and ethical responsibilities, and self-efficacy are related with environmental awareness, perceived social support, and green tech innovation, respectively. These factors then predicted bankers' niyyah toward issuing G-sukuk. The present research employed the theory of bounded rational planned behavior as its theoretical foundation. Data were collected from 390 bankers employed in different Islamic banks. Random sampling technique was employed for this cross-sectional study and for analyzing data, this study applied structural equation modeling. Findings indicate that all predictors are statistically significant and positively associated with bankers' niyyah toward G-sukuk for ensuring sustainable finance. Furthermore, G-sukuk initiatives can help to lower the carbon emissions and other harmful substances, which would improve overall environmental sustainability and ecological contexts related to SDG-13. There is limited empirical evidence available on the G-sukuk perspective in Bangladesh. This study will provide practical insights for the bankers and policymakers.

title: When Strong Enforcement Backfires: Breach Inducement and Contractual Governance
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, Advanced Institute of Business, Tongji University and Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

detail.title: When Strong Enforcement Backfires: Breach Inducement and Contractual Governance
detail.abstract: Firms commonly rely on fixed-price, fixed-quantity contracts to coordinate exchange, but uncertainty often renders these ex-ante commitments inefficient and prompts renegotiation. Renegotiation improves adaptability, but it also creates incentives for breach inducement: costly actions by one party that increase the counterparty's performance cost and improve the inducing party's ex-post bargaining position. We develop a buyer-seller model with two opposing ex-ante investments: the seller makes relationship-specific cost-reducing investment that increases trading surplus, while the buyer may undertake breach inducement, an opportunistic investment that distorts renegotiation incentives. We find three key results: (1) Expectation damages (ED), with flexible contract terms (high quantity and low price), align incentives, induce efficient investment, and suppress inducement (i.e., first-best outcome). (2) Specific performance (SP) can fail to achieve the first-best, especially when the seller's cost-reduction technology is sufficiently more scale sensitive than the buyer's inducement technology. In this regime, strong enforcement backfires because the contract point becomes a valuable renegotiation lever that encourages opportunistic inducement. (3) When contract terms are constrained and neither ED nor SP is generally first-best, liquidated damages (LD) serve as a hybrid governance instrument. LD is equivalent to SP when its stipulated fallback 1 is triggered in all states, but away from such extreme branches, its state-dependent fallback can mitigate inducement relative to SP. The comparison between LD and ED further depends on the renegotiation sharing rule: ED performs better when the buyer internalizes more of the surplus-reduction effect of inducement, whereas LD can perform better when the seller's bargaining share is sufficiently large. These findings help reconcile the theoretical appeal of strong enforcement with the practical prevalence of ED and LD, and they provide a remedy-selection framework for contracts that must balance investment protection, adaptation, and opportunism. The paper contributes to contractual governance by showing how breach remedies shape not only ex-post dispute resolution, but also ex-ante incentives in interfirm relationships.

title: When Oil Narratives Become Bank Risk

detail.title: When Oil Narratives Become Bank Risk
detail.abstract: Oil-market news can signal very different risks for banks exposed to oil-producing regions. This paper studies how newspaper-based oil narratives are associated with U.S. bank balance sheets. Supply-disruption narratives predict higher cumulative loan-loss provisions and net charge-offs, lower loan growth, lower deposit growth, and weaker short-run profitability among more oil-exposed banks. Demand-salience narratives move in the opposite direction, predicting stronger lending, deposit growth, and profitability, while provisions and charge-offs decline. These findings show that oil narratives do not have one banking effect: some oil stories become bank risk, while others coincide with expansion in oil-exposed banking markets.

title: Capturing The Value of Community Fuel Poverty Alleviation
affiliations: University of Sussex - Science and Technology Policy Research Unit (SPRU), University of Bristol and University of Bristol

detail.title: Capturing The Value of Community Fuel Poverty Alleviation
detail.abstract: This report summarises the findings of the ‘Capturing the value of community energy’ business collaboration project. We pursued a three-pronged approach to the data analysis. Firstly, we tried to establish comparability among the quantitative datasets to compare their approach, outreach and success in tackling fuel poverty. Secondly, we calculated the Social Return on Investment (SROI) using one specific dataset from 2018/19. Thirdly, we analysed the qualitative data to gain a deeper understanding of links between organisational approaches, fuel poverty alleviation interventions, data capture and management, and the funding environment. Due to complicated and highly variable reporting procedures it was only possible to establish comparable datasets on a few metrics which reflect requirements set by funders. The SROI calculation revealed that community fuel poverty alleviation efforts undertaken by the analysed companies has a SROI of 9-10:1 for every £1 invested. The qualitative analysis revealed the systematic underreporting of such value as funders’ targets are narrowly defined around numbers rather than genuinely lifting people out of fuel poverty. This report concludes with some recommendations to improve the operational environment for community fuel poverty alleviation services, especially given their invaluable efforts in reaching out to some of the most  vulnerable members of our communities.

title: Common Revisions, Relative Positions, and the Micro–Macro Wedge
affiliations: University of Auckland

detail.title: Common Revisions, Relative Positions, and the Micro–Macro Wedge
detail.abstract: Forecast-error-on-revision regressions have shaped a benchmark view of survey expectations: consensus forecasts appear to underreact to news, while individual forecasts appear to overreact. Using updated and aligned Survey of Professional Forecasters samples, I first show that this benchmark contrast is not stable across variables, horizons, and sample windows. I then show that the standard individual coefficient is a composite object: it places one slope on total individual revisions, which combine movements shared by forecasters with changes in forecasters' positions relative to the consensus. Decomposing these revisions shows that the shared component is the part of the individual regression with the usual consensus-style sign interpretation, varying across samples and macro episodes. The relativeposition component is more stable and negative, but it captures how relative forecast changes map into final relative forecasts, not an identified response to a particular information set. The weight on these components is the share of individual-revision variance accounted for by common movements. The individual coefficient is therefore a useful reduced-form statistic, but not a standalone test of behavioral bias.

title: The Inefficient Markets Hypothesis: A Theory of Casino Capitalism
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago

detail.title: The Inefficient Markets Hypothesis: A Theory of Casino Capitalism

publicationDetails.detailsText: FRB of Chicago Working Paper No. 2026-11
publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: I develop a general equilibrium model of investment and equity markets in which departures from the Efficient Markets Hypothesis generate "Casino Capitalism": time-inconsistent, short-termist firm decisions, firm-level over-investment coupled with inefficient liquidation of positive-NPV projects, and aggregate under-investment with depressed stock prices and distorted intertemporal savings. These distortions arise even if all agents are fully rational and forward-looking. At the firm level, the wedge between market-implied and fundamental returns on investment causes an endogenous preference reversal that renders the Laissez-faire outcome time-inconsistent and Pareto-inferior. In the aggregate, firm-level attempts to boost stock prices are self-defeating via an aggregate investment wedge as micro distortions translate into macro inefficiency. Restoring firm-level rationality by empowering shareholders can worsen aggregate outcomes and precipitate a complete capital market shutdown.

title: No-Questions-Asked, On-Chain: Deposit Disintermediation as a Moneyness Phase Transition

detail.title: No-Questions-Asked, On-Chain: Deposit Disintermediation as a Moneyness Phase Transition

keywords: Interest-Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB)

detail.abstract: Bank deposits are money because they are information-insensitive: they pass at par without the holder investigating the issuer, a property insurance and supervision confer. Tokenised money, whether bank-issued tokenised deposits or non-bank stablecoins, pursues the same property through verifiable reserves and at-par on-chain redemption. We place both in a logit (maximum-entropy) deposit-demand system with a salience threshold and a network complementarity in the outside option, and let banks price deposits optimally. The outside share obeys a mean-field self-consistency equation whose susceptibility diverges when responsiveness times coupling reaches βg = 4; beyond that the bare transition is first-order and hysteretic, but optimal defence holds the calibrated bank on a low plateau, so the migration is a latent threat rather than a realised run. The deposit beta is regime-dependent (flat on the rate floor, then full pass-through as banks defend), so defence caps outflow while turning the franchise into a zeroduration claim. Calibrated to Japan, corporate transactional deposits sit above the boundary and retail a sticky core. A core-deposit model fitted to the zero-rate era assigns the franchise a constant low beta and a long duration, so it books a large economic-value gain from rising rates and treats it as a rate hedge; this overstates the franchise's value (about 3.5-fold in the defended case) and credits a duration it lacks, leaving the bank under-hedged. The mis-measurement needs only the salience floor, with the coordination pulling lift-off into the supervisory shock window; where defence is imperfect it can instead turn the overstatement into an outright loss, of a size the historical beta cannot pin since the run-regime pass-through is out of sample. The robust message is that the transactional layer's rate risk is systematically mis-measured.

title: China's Rare Earth Policy: Prosperity Maximization or Great Power Geoeconomics?

detail.abstract: An industrial economics analysis of China’s quasi-monopoly on refined rare earth materials shows: even if China strictly maximizes national prosperity and abstains from geopolitical power play, a significant price differential emerges between the export price and the price for domestic users. The price differential itself is not evidence of geopolitical intentions. However, this equilibrium price gap widens if we assume that China views itself as contesting in a geopolitical, tournament-like situation against the United States. These two results are derived within the framework of a tournament model that imbeds the characteristics of a dominant supplier with a fringe - market, but adds geopolitical goals to the dominant supplier’s objective.

title: The Strategic Effect of Weak Team Members in Dynamic Conflicts between Teams
affiliations: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance

detail.title: The Strategic Effect of Weak Team Members in Dynamic Conflicts between Teams

publicationDetails.detailsText: Working Paper of the Max Planck Institute for Tax Law and Public Finance No. 2026-07
publicationDetails.journalName: Max Planck Institute for Tax Law & Public Finance Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Why do strong players allow weak players to join their team, even though weak players are notorious for free riding? This paper shows that the dynamic structure of a tug-of-war is suitable for mobilizing efforts by weak players and making the team to become stronger and to succeed. The strategic role of weak players emerges if the dynamics for the team develop unfavorably for the team. If the team falls behind, a discouragement effect sets in for the strong player. The player is inclined to throw the towel. This alarms the weak player. The player hoped to be able to free-ride and gain an expected windfall payoff. This payoff is lost if the strong player gives up. At that point the weak player actively seeks to motivate the strong player to perform at its best.

title: Luxury for All: A Macroeconomic Theory of Public Provision
affiliations: and Paris School of Economics (PSE)

detail.title: Luxury for All: A Macroeconomic Theory of Public Provision
detail.abstract: Public in-kind provision of education, healthcare, or cultural amenities accounts for a large share of government spending, even though redistribution can be achieved with cash transfers and externalities addressed with subsidies. We propose a new macroeconomic theory of in-kind provision, grounded in two features: (i) these goods are luxuries, with consumption rising more than proportionally with income; and (ii) they generate externalities that depend not only on the total level of consumption but also on its distribution across households. In a tractable heterogeneous-agent model, we show that these features make direct in-kind provision welfare-improving, even when cash transfers and subsidies are available. Using household- and country-level data, we document that most publicly provided goods exhibit both features. We then apply the framework to the design of fiscal consolidation, showing in a calibrated model that optimal consolidation falls primarily on goods without private substitutes, while preserving in-kind provision of goods with private substitutes. Finally, we develop a welfare-based imputation method for in-kind benefits, to provide a more accurate assessment of the distributional impact of government spending.

title: Task-Specific Technical Change and Comparative Advantage
affiliations: Stanford University and Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) - Centre de Recerca en Economia Internacional (CREI)

detail.title: Task-Specific Technical Change and Comparative Advantage
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes workers’ comparative advantage by altering the tasks they perform and the skills those tasks require. We develop a dynamic task-based model to quantify the general-equilibrium effects of task-specific technical change. Workers have multidimensional skills, choose occupations, and accumulate skills on the job; occupations combine tasks, and productivity depends on how workers’ skills match task requirements. We develop a computationally efficient procedure to estimate the model using panel data and a new database of task-level skill requirements. We apply the model to AI, allowing it to augment, automate, and simplify tasks. We find that AI narrows wage inequality and raises average wages across scenarios ranging from slow to rapid AI progress. The key equalizing force is simplification: by lowering tasks’ skill requirements, AI lets lower-skill workers compete for previously inaccessible jobs. Adoption costs, highest for lower-skill workers, dampen but do not eliminate the decline in inequality.

title: To Combine or Not? Consolidating Horizontal Acquisitions in Multi-sided Market
affiliations: Stevens Institute of Technology

detail.title: To Combine or Not? Consolidating Horizontal Acquisitions in Multi-sided Market
detail.abstract: When a parent company acquires a horizontal competitor on the same side of a multi-sided market, it must decide whether to fully integrate the acquired platform or keep it as a separate brand. We study this in the context of Uber’s acquisition of Postmates, using novel consumer receipt data that tracks food delivery spending. Employing an Age–Period–Cohort (APC) decomposition, we isolate the merger’s effect on consumer spending while controlling for lifecycle and cohort effects. We find that Postmates users sharply reduced their spending on the platform after the merger, but spending shifted not only to UberEats, but also to competitors like DoorDash and Grubhub. Consumers who used multiple platforms and had low pre-merger activity on Postmates were more "sticky", showing little change. Comparing our APC results with a standard Difference-in-Differences (DiD) design, we find the DiD underestimates the merger’s total impact by missing market-wide effects. Our findings suggest that in multi-sided markets, keeping acquired platforms separate can be beneficial; dissolving them may push demand to competitors, and some sticky multihoming users may not shift spending at all.

title: The Perceived Inflation Wedge
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill

detail.title: The Perceived Inflation Wedge
detail.abstract:
Standard measures of inflation, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), are designed to measure changes in the cost of living, not how households perceive price changes under limited attention and imperfect information. This paper introduces Perceived Inflation (PI), an attention-weighted inflation measure derived from a model in which households allocate attention across goods and observe noisy price signals. I construct monthly PI using disaggregated CPI data and attention proxies based on price salience, volatility, media mentions, and search behavior. The resulting PI series is highly correlated with CPI inflation but exhibits greater short-run volatility, especially during the Global Financial Crisis, the COVID-19 recession, and the 2021–22 inflation surge. A state-space version of the index implies a persistent latent attention component and a time-varying PI wedge. Finally, the paper embeds the estimated PI wedge into a heterogeneous-household model to demonstrate how attention-driven distortions in inflation perceptions affect saving and consumption through perceived real returns.

title: To Catch a Thief: Endogenous Policing and Choice of Location by Criminals
affiliations: University of Birmingham - Department of Economics,  and University College London - Department of Economics

detail.title: To Catch a Thief: Endogenous Policing and Choice of Location by Criminals
detail.abstract: This paper develops a tractable model of offender location choice and police resource allocation across multiple areas. Individuals differ in the cost of apprehension and choose whether to commit crime and, if so, where. Each area contains a fixed value of criminal opportunities, so offenders impose congestion on one another, while policing affects expected apprehension. For arbitrary policing levels, equilibrium sorts offenders by apprehension cost across areas ordered by policing per unit of criminal opportunity value. With a fixed police budget, welfare maximization equalizes policing-to-value ratios across all active areas. The model shows when place-based policing should target the value of criminal opportunities rather than observed crime counts alone, since observed crime may already reflect prior police allocation and offender displacement.

title: Dynamic Charitable Giving
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance & Management, , Frankfurt School of Finance & Management and

detail.title: Dynamic Charitable Giving
detail.abstract: This paper studies the dynamics of charitable giving. We model giving as the accumulation of virtue capital from past giving and test the model using panel data linking 7.6 million donations to 52 fundraising letters over six years. Giving is intertemporally consistent: past giving breeds future giving, past inaction breeds future inaction. This negative consistency quantitatively dominates: fundraising appeals cause negative intertemporal spillovers on subsequent appeals. However, negative consistency fades more quickly than positive consistency. These results contribute to our understanding of dynamic prosocial behavior and inform how fundraising campaigns should time and sequence communications.

title: Panel Attrition, Data Imputation and Age Patterns in Subjective Ill-being
affiliations: Dartmouth College - Department of Economics, University College London and Dartmouth College

detail.title: Panel Attrition, Data Imputation and Age Patterns in Subjective Ill-being
detail.abstract:
We examine the implications of panel attrition for the age profile of subjective ill-being in the Global Flourishing Study (GFS). We establish that survey attrition rates are high, and are highest among the young, particularly when interviewed in wave 1 using a computer-assisted web interview (CAWI). We then deploy three methods (inverse probability weighting, multiple imputation chain equations, and last observation carried forward) to estimate the age pattern in subjective ill-being in wave 2 of the survey. All three methods have their strengths and weaknesses, but we demonstrate that such adjustments are merited given the nature of survey attrition in the data. We conclude that subjective ill-being is declining in age in both waves 1 and 2 of the GFS having accounted for sample attrition, something that would not have been apparent if one simply ran wave 2 regressions without accounting for sample attrition.

title: Trading Frictions in Dynamic Cap-and-Trade Markets
affiliations: LUISS University - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Rochester, Yale University, Yale University - Cowles Foundation and University of California, Berkeley - Haas School of Business

detail.title: Trading Frictions in Dynamic Cap-and-Trade Markets
detail.abstract:
We develop a dynamic stochastic model of markets with an externality and multiple trading frictions, and cap-and-trade as the leading application. Slow participation, limited intermediation, and heterogeneous information interact in equilibrium: agents choose costly market access, access determines residual compliance demand, intermediary constraints translate residual demand into a surrender-month premium, and the premium feeds back into access incentives. These interactions shape how effectively the market corrects the externality. We characterize access choices in closed form, prove that the equilibrium premium is unique, and show that endogenous access dampens the response to each friction in isolation, while the interaction of multiple frictions is non-additive and can amplify the price response. We quantify the model using 2.7 million EU ETS registry transactions and compliance records from 2005–2021. About 40% of operators do not trade annually, purchases concentrate in April when returns are systematically high, and operator flow predicts future returns.

title: Pension Income and Post-Retirement Labor Supply
affiliations: University of Regensburg, , ,  and Karlsruhe Institute of Technology

detail.title: Pension Income and Post-Retirement Labor Supply
detail.abstract: This paper provides causal evidence on how pension income affects labor supply after retirement. We exploit the introduction of the German Earned Income Pension Credit (Grundrente), which permanently increased pension income for retirees with long contribution histories and comparatively low lifetime earnings. The reform generates exogenous variation in non-labor income without creating additional labor supply distortions, allowing us to isolate pure income effects. Using administrative data covering the universe of German retirees and a difference-in-differences design, we find that a 1,200 euro increase in annual pension income reduces unconditional labor earnings by approximately 122 euros, implying a marginal propensity to earn out of unearned income of −0.1. Two thirds of this response reflects extensive margin adjustments, which operate through both increased exit and reduced re-entry, with the remainder driven by intensive margin reductions. Effects are stronger for younger, more labor-market-attached cohorts.

title: Mathematical Modelling of Hepatitis B in the Context of Evolutionary Game Theory
affiliations: Akenten Appiah-Menka University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (AAMUSTED)

detail.title: Mathematical Modelling of Hepatitis B in the Context of Evolutionary Game Theory
detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between vaccination, disease transmission, and individual be havioral reactions using a fractional order model in conjunction with evolutionary game dynamics. The Atangana Baleanu Caputo (ABC) fractional derivative is used in the hepatitis B model formulation to account for memory effects. We prove the model fundamental mathematical characteristics, such as pos itivity and boundedness of solutions. The basic reproduction number is used to examine the local and global stability of the disease-free and endemic equilibria. Theoretical findings are corroborated using numerical simulations, which also show how fractional memory, vaccination cost, and vaccine efficiency affect behavioral and epidemic dynamics. The findings emphasize how crucial behavioral and memory elements are to successful Hepatitis B control.

title: Information Provision and Demand-Side Barriers to Healthcare Innovation: Experimental Evidence on Shared Medical Appointments in Menopause Care
affiliations: School of Economics, University of Edinburgh, University College London, University of Oxford, University of Virginia - Department of Economics and London Business School - Department of Management Science and Operations

detail.title: Information Provision and Demand-Side Barriers to Healthcare Innovation: Experimental Evidence on Shared Medical Appointments in Menopause Care
detail.abstract:
Alternative care delivery models may offer benefits to patients and providers, but adoption often remains low. We study whether brief narrative testimonials shift willingness to attend virtual shared medical appointments (SMAs), a relatively little-used care format in which 5-15 patients with a shared non-urgent health condition meet simultaneously with a clinician. Using a pre-registered field experiment with over 4,000 women aged 45–60 in the UK, we randomly assigned participants to view only standard descriptive information about menopause appointment options (the control group) or to receive testimonials about SMAs from either previous patients or a clinician (treatment groups). Testimonials more than doubled the share of women choosing an SMA: when appointments were offered with a 6-8 week wait, 11% of the control group chose an SMA compared to 26% in the peer testimonials arm and 24% in the clinician testimonials arm. Shorter waiting times further increase uptake. When the SMA wait was reduced to one week, the share of women ever choosing an SMA rose by 14-19 percentage points across arms, reaching nearly 40% in the testimonial groups. Treatment effects are systematically larger among women with greater information-processing capacity: university education, higher baseline menopause knowledge, and broader information-seeking. Our findings suggest that women’s reluctance to choose SMAs is driven primarily by demand-side barriers, including unfamiliarity and uncertainty about their benefits, rather than deep-seated aversion to group-based care. Testimonials appear sufficient to meaningfully reduce these barriers.

title: Rising Replacement Burden and the Compression of Net Building

detail.title: Rising Replacement Burden and the Compression of Net Building
detail.abstract: The share of output absorbed by replacing depreciating productive structure — the ratio of the consumption of fixed capital to output, 𝛿 = CFC/𝑌 — has risen steadily across every major economy since 1950. We establish three things. First, the rise is a robust and physical fact: it holds across US national accounts (1929–2025), a 180-country Penn World Table panel (1950–2023), and OECD STAN industry data (1970–2023); it survives a purely real construction that removes all nominal prices; and it is invariant to the depreciation-accounting method national agencies use. Second, the rise tightens an accounting constraint. Because the gross investment share is bounded (Kaldor 1961), a rising 𝛿 compresses the residual available for net new building, 𝑛 = 𝐶/𝑌 − 𝛿; in Japan this residual has fallen to 2.5% of GDP, the closest empirical approach to a replacement trap in which replacement absorbs all gross investment and net building reaches zero. Third, the rise decomposes — through the identity 𝛿 = (CFC/𝐾) × (𝐾/𝑌 ) — into a composition channel (faster-depreciating capital) and a scale channel (deeper accumulation); the United States is compositionled and Japan scale-led, with the intermediate cases sensitive to valuation and best read as qualitative. We stop at the net building rate. Whether the compressed 𝑛 slows productivity growth runs through a transmission coefficient whose magnitude is debated in the growth-accounting literature and which we do not identify; we establish the measurement and the identity, and leave the causal step to subsequent work.

title: Assessing Growth and Inflationary Implications of India's Carbon Credit Trading System: A Social Cost of Carbon Approach
affiliations: Independent and Power Management Institute India

detail.title: Assessing Growth and Inflationary Implications of India's Carbon Credit Trading System: A Social Cost of Carbon Approach
detail.abstract: This study evaluates the impact of proposed emission trading system in India on growth and inflation using the social cost of carbon approach. We use a novel measure the latent carbon price which we shows is similar to social cost of carbon due to adverse impact of global warming on total factor productivity. Our three-step procedure to evaluate the India’s proposed emission trading system consists of estimating the latent carbon price using KELMS data and robust regression methods. The estimated average latent carbon price as per the current sectoral coverage is $101.43 per tonne and $59.24 per tonne when sectoral coverage is hypothetically expanded to include electricity and iron & steel. Using Leontief price and demand equation the average impact on inflation and output is not high for current sectoral coverage of and is estimated at 0.05 per cent and 0.13 per cent respectively with green sacrifice ratio of $568.98 per tonne of emission reduction. However, inclusion of electricity and iron & steel in expected to be inflationary. The inflation is expected to rise to 0.15 per cent and output negatively impacted by 0.35 per cent. The green sacrifice ratio is lower at and $310.16 per tonne of emission reduction. Sectors that are impacted most outside the emission trading system sectors include financial intermediation, construction, air transport and mining and quarrying. Study highlights that rise of competitive imports in sectors not covered under emission trading system can further negatively impact these sectors and needs more closer examination from policy point of view to minimize the cost of transition.

title: Foreign Involvement in Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Foreign Involvement in Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism
detail.abstract: Africa is inundated with Western actors seeking to counter and prevent violent extremism (Ismael & Skons 2014). Interest in Africa has revived for various reasons. Some actors are in Africa to access its natural resources, while others are concerned about the transnational threats that originate from Africa. Some, such as Brazil, China, and Russia, are emerging powers, some are former colonial masters, and others are non-state actors (Ebo 2007). Each of these are developing different types of relations with the AU, individual African countries, RECs, and local organisations. In spite of all African countries attaining independence several decades ago, a myriad of foreign actors continue to influence its security landscape. Some provide technical support, capacity-building, joint military operations, and intelligence-gathering (ibid). There are a number of scholarly works on the role of Western actors in broad area of peace and security (Brosig 2010; Ebo 2007; Van Genugten 2008), but less so on foreign involvement in PCVE in Africa. This chapter is an attempt to help fill this gap. It provides an overview of international action in countering and preventing VE in Africa. It examines the origins and nature of international actors in PCVE in Africa, and asks whose interests they really serve. Partnerships with local actors and the overall impact of the involvements are also addressed. The chapter argues that Africa’s own attempt to curb VE with the assistance of foreign actors has failed, largely due to the assumption that Africa is homogeneous and that one policy approach will therefore fit all countries. In reality, African countries are shaped by seemingly similar yet different historical and structural factors and actors. The lack of agreement on the standards for evaluating PVE and CVE programmes in Africa has further made it difficult to register meaningful success in countering and preventing VE. RECs such as SADC need to play a leading role in ensuring that monitoring and evaluation take account of local realities. We need to note that involvement in CVE/PVE is not apolitical in the sense that foreign actors influence local politics as they strive to achieve their own interests. Similarly, foreign actors are shaped by the politics of the state in cases where African states engage in rent-seeking behaviour.

title: Pay for Dirt or for Green? The Moderating Role of Institutional Quality in Transitioning Economies
affiliations: University of North Georgia

detail.title: Pay for Dirt or for Green? The Moderating Role of Institutional Quality in Transitioning Economies
detail.abstract: To date, most of the existing literature has examined how bribery and innovation affect firm productivity, while paying limited attention to the reverse causal relationship. This paper addresses this gap by studying firms in transitioning economies during the 2010s, with a particular focus on green research and development (R&D). We empirically investigate how firm productivity influences bribery behavior and two distinct green R&D strategies: independent innovation and dependent imitation. Our results show that more productive firms are more likely to engage in bribery and less likely to invest in green R&D overall. Conditional on undertaking green R&D, however, higher productivity increases the likelihood of innovation while reducing reliance on imitation. Additionally, the impact of productivity is significantly moderated by institutional quality. Under poor institutional quality characterized by substantial infrastructural and bureaucratic obstacles, the positive effect of productivity on bribery and its negative effect on green R&D-particularly green innovation-are significantly amplified.

title: Shares in Students: A New Model for University Funding
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Shares in Students: A New Model for University Funding
detail.abstract:
UK higher education faces an acute funding crisis. The government's marginal increase in tuition fees, rising from £9,250 to £9,535 in 2025, generates only £330 million, falling short of the £370 million burden created by its own budget, leaving many institutions on the brink of financial failure and threatening the UK's standing as a world-class higher education provider.

At the root of this crisis lies an outdated, centralised funding model, a legacy of the post-1918 Haldane Report, which has progressively eroded universities' financial independence. Crucially, because the government issues student loans and absorbs repayment risk, universities face incentives to prioritise recruitment over graduate employability. The result is growing enrolments but poor outcomes, with one in five graduates earning less than they would have without a degree.

This paper proposes a fundamental restructuring of university finance. The cap on tuition fees would be abolished, and the government loan amount would be frozen. Universities would set fees according to market demand, financing any amount above the government loan through income-contingent agreements issued by the institution itself rather than the state. Drawing on the master-apprentice tradition, this arrangement ensures that universities prosper financially only if their graduates do, incentivising institutions to recruit students ready for serious study and to design courses that lead to genuine workplace success.

Recognising the public benefit of university assets, the paper further proposes that the state become owner and shareholder, with universities listed on the London Stock Exchange, potentially raising in the order of £100 billion for the Exchequer. Taken together, these reforms would realign incentives across the sector, improve student outcomes, restore fiscal sustainability, and position the UK as the global leader in higher education.

title: Private Equity and Venture Capital : Understanding the Investment Spectrum
affiliations: Multimedia University (MMU)

detail.title: Private Equity and Venture Capital : Understanding the Investment Spectrum
detail.abstract: In The Key Takeaways : Private Equity and Venture Capital (2025), the learned author distilled the key distinctions, similarities and the fundamental mechanics governing the deployment of capital in Private Equity (PE) and Venture Capital (VC) within the modern investment system. This article explores further in relation to the managerial process that drives investment decisions, and the deal-making frameworks that determine price and return. Understanding these concepts is essential for appreciating how private capital investors identify opportunities, manage risk, and create value throughout the investment lifecycle.

title: Natural Disasters, Government Safety Nets, and Household Portfolio Choice
affiliations: Zicklin School of Business, Baruch College - The City University of New York, City University of New York, Baruch College - Zicklin School of Business - Department of Economics and Finance and

detail.title: Natural Disasters, Government Safety Nets, and Household Portfolio Choice
detail.abstract: Using a nationwide survey spanning 2011 to 2019, we find that natural disasters reduce household stock market participation and risky asset allocation. These effects are substantially mitigated, by 58 to 75%, following the introduction of two government insurance programs that improve healthcare access and disaster risk sharing. For identification, we exploit the staggered provincial rollout of the healthcare program and use peer province disaster experience as a plausibly exogenous shock, along with household fixed effects and falsification tests. We further document heterogeneous effects: the adverse impacts of disasters are more pronounced among poorer, uninsured, and less financially sophisticated households. Our evidence suggests that effective policies can buffer the adverse financial impacts of disasters, thereby improving household financial resilience. Households also express a preference for public over private insurance programs in response to disaster losses.

title: Tainted Debt Is Not Enforceable Debt — Policy Brief: Why the USD 150–170 Billion Reference Stock Is a Legally Illegitimate Figure and the Indispensable Role of the Egmont Group in Venezuela's Restructuring

detail.abstract: This policy brief presents the principal findings and policy recommendations of the technical research paper "Tainted Debt Is Not Enforceable Debt" (CESV Spain Chapter / Riskoff, June 2026) [SSRN No. pending]. It argues that the USD 150–170 billion reference stock used in Venezuela's sovereign debt restructuring is not fully enforceable debt, introduces a tripartite legal classification of the bond inventory under New York law, identifies three cumulative legal consequences for holders of tainted debt, and advances five technical recommendations centred on the formal activation of the Egmont Group's 176 financial intelligence units as the indispensable mechanism for a legally valid exchange offer.

title: The Disposition Effect under Uncertainty: An Information Processing Perspective
affiliations: and University College London

detail.title: The Disposition Effect under Uncertainty: An Information Processing Perspective

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was approved by the University College London Research Ethics Committee (Ethical Approval Number: EP/2023/012), and informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the experiment.

detail.abstract: The disposition effect—the tendency to sell assets at a gain more readily than those at a loss—is among the most stable behavioural biases in financial decision-making. Although typically attributed to Prospect Theory, this explanation faces two significant challenges: (1) Prospect Theory does not adequately account for investment decisions under uncertainty (as opposed to risk), and (2) empirical evidence linking Prospect Theory to the disposition effect remains inconsistent. In this study, we propose an alternative explanation based on an information processing perspective. Across two controlled experiments (N = 125), we observed a significant disposition effect that was more pronounced under uncertainty than under known risk, and further exacerbated by higher volatility. By applying a cognitive model that treats decision-making as evidence accumulation toward a threshold (the shifted Wald model), we found that participants exhibited higher information processing efficiency in the gain domain compared to the loss domain. Furthermore, participants adopted higher decision thresholds in the gain domain than in the loss domain under risk only, but behaved in largely opposite patterns under uncertainty. These findings underscore the importance of investigating the cognitive foundations of investor behaviour in realistic scenarios and offer new insights into the mechanisms underlying the disposition effect.

title: Financial Constraints, Export Dynamics, and R&D Strategies: Firm-Level Evidence from Global Emerging Economies
affiliations: University of North Georgia

detail.title: Financial Constraints, Export Dynamics, and R&D Strategies: Firm-Level Evidence from Global Emerging Economies
detail.abstract: This paper empirically examines how financial constraints affect firms' dynamic exporting behavior and how R&D strategies serve as an important transmission channel. Using panel data constructed from the World Bank Enterprise Surveys during 2013-2023 across multiple emerging economies, we employ a twostage estimation to address endogeneity and simultaneity error. We reveal that financial constraint is associated with significantly lower likelihood of both export entry and export persistence, reaffirming the importance of financial flexibility in sustaining international activities. Notably, we identify R&D as the key mechanism. Successful R&D substantially attenuates the negative association between financial constraints and export entry, and partially attenuates this relationship for continuing exporters. Further distinguishing between two R&D strategies, we find that innovation is more sensitive to financial factors than imitation. Moreover, imitation facilitates export entry, whereas innovation supports export persistence. These findings provide new insights into the R&D-export nexus and highlight that easing financing frictions is critical for enabling firms to convert R&D investment into export capability and long-term international competitiveness.

title: Morals and the Political Economy of Corrective Taxes
affiliations: University of Cologne - Center for Macroeconomic Research (CMR), Vanderbilt University - College of Arts and Science - Department of Economics,  and Humboldt University Berlin

detail.title: Morals and the Political Economy of Corrective Taxes
detail.abstract: We study the political economy of carbon taxes when neoclassical consumers take all other agents' emissions as given and socially responsible consumers internalize damages in a group-rule-utilitarian way, taking neoclassical consumers' behavior as given. We characterize political equilibrium taxes with a focus on deviations from first-best Pigouvian taxation. Welfare falls further if arguments on moral obligations to reduce carbon footprints polarize the debate in society. Finally, we present survey evidence that supports our theory: social responsibility correlates with lower consumption of brown goods, higher preferred carbon taxes, and support for moral arguments.

title:
From balance sheet arithmetic to cognitive capture: a neurodigital theory of uncontrolled consumption and insolvency 
Induction

detail.title:
From balance sheet arithmetic to cognitive capture: a neurodigital theory of uncontrolled consumption and insolvency 
Induction
detail.abstract: This article proposes a radical rereading of insolvency in the algorithmic era, where financial decisions no longer emerge from a rational subject, but from a heuristic debtor shaped by digital architectures that exploit cognitive and affective vulnerabilities. The convergence between consumer, investment and betting platforms has transformed indebtedness into an emotionally induced and technologically directed process. In this environment, algorithmic opacity, gamification, and the elimination of transactional frictions erode the economic autonomy of the individual. Thus, insolvency ceases to be a mere equity imbalance to become the foreseeable outcome of an ecosystem that manufactures "winners who lose" and digitizes assets, subjecting them to tokenization and conditional liquidity logics. The article argues that classic bankruptcy law is insufficient to address this reality, so it proposes to integrate neuroscience, behavioral economics and algorithmic studies as pillars of a new regulatory design capable of confronting the structural manipulation of financial behavior.

title: Online Data Processing Under GATS Section 2.C.n

detail.title: Online Data Processing Under GATS Section 2.C.n
detail.abstract:
Brazil's General Data Protection Law (LGPD, Lei 13.709/2018) and the Marco Civil da Internet Article 11 (Lei 12.965/2014) impose conditions on cross-border transfers of personal data that restrict the ability of foreign service suppliers to deliver online data processing services from outside Brazilian territory. This paper examines whether these measures raise questions of tension with Brazil's specific commitments under the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS), as inscribed in GATS/SC/13/Suppl.2 — Brazil's schedule of specific commitments under the Fourth Protocol on Basic Telecommunications (1997). Under Section 2.C.n of the W/120 services classification framework, Brazil consolidated full market access ("None") for Modes 1, 2, and 3 in online data processing and value-added telecommunications services. This commitment predates the LGPD by twenty-one years and the Marco Civil by seventeen years.

Three independent lines of analysis are examined: (i) Article XVI:2(c) GATS, which prohibits numerical limitations on service supply where "None" has been committed; (ii) Article VI:5 GATS, which addresses measures enacted after a commitment that nullify its benefit without constituting an Article XVI restriction; and (iii) Article II GATS (Most-Favoured-Nation), a line of inquiry prompted by ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD No. 32/2026 (January 26, 2026), which granted adequacy status exclusively to the European Union without extending equivalent treatment to other WTO Members. The paper further examines the GATS Annex on Telecommunications, Paragraph 5(c), which guarantees the movement of information and access to data in machine-readable form across borders — a provision directly applicable to cross-border data processing services.

Brazil's Article XIV(c) privacy exception defense is examined against the necessity test established in US-Gambling (WT/DS285/AB/R, 2005), and against the chapeau's prohibition on arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination — though, as discussed in Section 5.2, resolving the chapeau question would require a separate factual determination of whether EU and US service suppliers operate under "like conditions," which this paper does not undertake. The EU's GDPR framework — which appears to achieve equivalent data protection objectives without data localization — is identified as a documented, potentially less-restrictive alternative. The USTR's Section 301 determination of June 1, 2026 explicitly declined to reach conclusions on the actionability of Brazil's data transfer restrictions, leaving open a distinct analytical pathway under the GATS framework that this paper examines. This paper does not purport to resolve whether Brazil's measures are in fact inconsistent with its WTO obligations; it identifies a previously underexplored analytical question warranting further examination (see Scope and Legal Position, below).

title: Oil fairness, Subsistence demand, and Optimal Policy

detail.title: Oil fairness, Subsistence demand, and Optimal Policy
detail.abstract: Oil prices are easy to observe and hard to interpret. The household sees the posted price, not the firm's marginal cost, and must decide how much of any increase reflects cost pressure and how much reflects a higher markup. This inference matters especially for oil because part of consumption is non-discretionary: a household may judge a posted price unfair and still buy what it needs for commuting or heating. I study this interaction in a two-sector model with a sticky-price non-oil sector and a flexible-price oil sector. Households infer perceived marginal costs from observed prices and past perceived costs, and perceived markups determine the fairness assigned to each posted price. Oil demand has a Stone-Geary-type structure, so only the discretionary part responds to perceived unfairness. Fairness and subsistence enter through the elasticity faced by oil firms, but they pull in opposite directions. Fairness raises the elasticity of discretionary demand because a price increase is partly read as an unfair-pricing signal. Subsistence lowers the share of total demand that can respond. The elasticity of total oil demand is therefore the product of the fairness-amplified discretionary elasticity and the discretionary demand share. Fairness alone lowers the oil markup below the standard New Keynesian benchmark. Subsistence can pull it back to the benchmark or push it above, depending on the discretionary share. The same logic governs Ramsey policy. At moderate fairness, the optimal labor instrument is a smaller subsidy than in the benchmark. When fairness is strong and oil is sufficiently essential, the labor subsidy turns into a tax.

title: Banking Deregulation and Consumption Insurance. E Case of Italy in the Early 1990s

detail.title: Banking Deregulation and Consumption Insurance. E Case of Italy in the Early 1990s

contentType.other: revised chapter from a doctoral dissertation/thesis

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates whether Italian banking deregulation in the early 1990s affected households’ consumption insurance. Using the Bank of Italy’s Survey of Household Income and Wealth (SHIW), the analysis exploits the substantial heterogeneity across households to examine whether structural banking reforms — including the privatisation of the banking sector, the removal of branching restrictions, and the reintroduction of universal banking — altered households’ ability to smooth consumption in response to unanticipated income shocks within a partial insurance framework. The results suggest that banking deregulation significantly improved households’ ability to insure against unanticipated permanent income shocks, while no statistically significant effects are found for transitory shocks. The paper also contributes to identifying the main transmission channels through which banking deregulation influenced household consumption insurance.

title: “Nash Equilibria and Dilemmas of Accountability: A Study of Diplomatic and Criminal Survival Strategies from the Presidency to the Post-Presidency in the DRC”

detail.title: “Nash Equilibria and Dilemmas of Accountability: A Study of Diplomatic and Criminal Survival Strategies from the Presidency to the Post-Presidency in the DRC”

This study was conducted independently and is purely academic, with no partisan or institutional alignment with any political or judicial actors in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

The research is strictly based on the conceptual analysis of publicly available legal texts, historical documentation, and mathematical modeling.
