detail.abstract: This study analyzes the mechanisms of criminal, political, and diplomatic accountability of Joseph Kabila through an innovative, interdisciplinary approach that combines international law, political science, and mathematical modeling. The core of the analysis rests on the concept of the "rebellion pattern," viewed not as a past historical state, but as a latent power structure and an active technology of deterrence. By leveraging game theory, this study demonstrates that the political transition in the Democratic Republic of the Congo produced a stable Nash equilibrium. In this state, the successor government waives judicial prosecution to guarantee institutional stability, while the former leader limits his disruptive capacity as long as his de facto immunity is respected. The application of jurimetrics, via the accountability function Res, confirms that the actor's deterrent power ($Pd$) neutralizes the effectiveness of the legal norm. The findings corroborate Zartman's theory on conflict ripeness: in hybrid states, legality is structurally subordinate to stability. Impunity does not emerge as a systemic failure, but rather as a mathematically calculated cost for maintaining a fragile peace in the Great Lakes region. Ultimately, diplomatic accountability remains a geopolitical adjustment variable, fluctuating according to the imperatives of regional security rather than the principles of universal justice.

title: The Sen Liberal Paradox at Family Scale: A Kernel-Checked Proof-Layer Lift, Its Witness/Audit Boundary, and a Transfer Contract

detail.title: The Sen Liberal Paradox at Family Scale: A Kernel-Checked Proof-Layer Lift, Its Witness/Audit Boundary, and a Transfer Contract
detail.abstract: Finite impossibility witnesses in social choice theory are increasingly delivered as proofcarrying artifacts: a kernel-checked Lean theorem at a base case, plus a CNF certificate audited at the same base case. When such a witness is generalised to a case family, "the witness transferred" is not one claim but two-a Proof-layer transfer of the semantic argument, and a Witness/Audit-layer transfer of the CNF encoding that backed the original certificate-and the two come apart. We demonstrate this layer split for Sen's Liberal Paradox by pairing a kernel-checked positive answer at the Lean Proof layer with an explicit scope wall against the CNF Witness/Audit layer. Concretely, we formalise and verify sen_impossibility_lifts: for any finite case with at least two voters and at least four alternatives, any social welfare function satisfying semantic unanimity (UN) and minimal liberalism (MINLIB) fails SocialAcyclic. The proof ports the Sen24 base-case case-split (two-overlap, one-overlap, disjoint) at the semantic axiom level; its overlap case analysis avoids any universal four-point completion in Fin m, so the hypothesis 4 ≤ m is not consumed. On the negative side, the Lean lift does not automatically upgrade the sen24 CNF certificate into a family-level one: the Witness/Audit layer certifies only the sen24-audited short-cycle encoding no_cycle3 ∧ no_cycle4, whose equivalence to full acyclicity was audited only at four alternatives, and for m ≥ 5 that equivalence does not transfer automatically. The contribution is therefore a Transfer Contract: proof-level transfer is kernel-checked and reaches full acyclicity, while witness-level transfer requires a separately audited encoding contract.

title: The Evolution of Luxury Signaling

detail.title: The Evolution of Luxury Signaling
detail.abstract: Luxury consumption has long been synonymous with social status, distinction, and prestige. This literature review examines how the meaning and mechanisms of luxury signaling have changed over time. Beginning with Thorstein Veblen's theory of conspicuous consumption, the paper explains how visible indicators of wealth historically functioned as symbols of prestige. It then analyzes the contributions of Bagwell and Bernheim, whose work demonstrates that luxury goods derive value not only from their function but also from their ability to signal status through price. The review further investigates the rise of quiet luxury, drawing on the work of Han, Nunes, and Drèze to explain why many affluent consumers increasingly prefer quiet forms of luxury over huge displays of wealth. Finally, connecting with the digital era ,the paper examines how digital technologies, social media, and virtual assets have transformed contemporary status signaling by creating new forms of visibility, attention, and symbolic value. The review finds that while the methods of signaling have shifted from conspicuous logos to more knowledge-based forms of distinction, the underlying hunger for social status remains largely unchanged. Luxury consumption continues to function as a powerful means of communicating status, although the signals themselves have become increasingly abstruse in this era.

title: Equilibrium Self-Selection in Pass-Fail Tests
affiliations: University of Turin - Department of Economics

detail.title: Equilibrium Self-Selection in Pass-Fail Tests
detail.abstract: Whether taking an optional pass-fail test is optimal depends on pass probabilities, which increase in productivity and are each individual's private information, and on the wages earned when passing or failing the test, which are conditional expectations formed about productivity by employers who know its distribution in the population subset that chooses to take the test. This paper models the relevant rational-expectations equilibrium and shows that plausible pass-probability functions imply that as a difficult test becomes more difficult, taking it becomes more appealing for low-productivity individuals who are likely to fail. Along with other features of real-life tests, this rationalizes the very low success rates of some optional admission and publication processes.

title: Political Ideology, Environmental Policy Adaptation, and Greenhouse Gas Emissions
affiliations: , Thompson Rivers University and Thompson Rivers University

detail.title: Political Ideology, Environmental Policy Adaptation, and Greenhouse Gas Emissions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no financial or non‐financial conflicts of interest related to this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge financial support from the Sustainability Research Cluster, Bob Gaglardi School of Business and Economics, Thompson Rivers University, which funded the hiring of a research assistant for this project.

detail.abstract: It is widely believed that the willingness to adopt stringent environmental and energy policies, as well as to participate in global climate agreements, is influenced by the political ideology of the party in power. This paper examines how political ideology affects both the adoption and effectiveness of environmental policies, including energy policies, in reducing greenhouse gas emissions (GHGE) across OECD countries. Specifically, we investigate whether the political ideology of ruling parties influences a country's decision to join the global climate action agenda, pursue domestic climate initiatives, and how these choices translate into measurable emission reductions. Using panel data for 31 OECD countries from 1995 to 2021, we employ contemporaneous, lag, and threshold models within the STIRPAT framework. We find no significant evidence that political ideology alone determines the adoption of global environmental policies. However, when coupled with strong domestic and global environmental policy adaptation and implementation, political ideology contributes significantly to reductions in GHGE. These results are robust across models and alternative estimation techniques. Our findings highlight the economic and policy importance of moving beyond symbolic participation toward genuine climate action, aligning national energy policies with international commitments, and integrating political economy considerations into climate policy design.

title: To what Extent has the Single-use Plastic (SUP) ban Implemented by Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB), in 2022 Helped Reduce the Overconsumption of Single-use Plastic?

detail.title: To what Extent has the Single-use Plastic (SUP) ban Implemented by Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB), in 2022 Helped Reduce the Overconsumption of Single-use Plastic?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Survey data was collected voluntarily and anonymously via Google Forms. No formal ethics approval was required.

detail.abstract:
Bengaluru generates over 600 tonnes of plastic waste every single day. Despite this, the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board's 2022 ban on single-use plastics has received surprisingly little academic attention. This paper attempts to fill that gap by asking a simple question: has the ban actually worked?

Drawing on a survey of 104 Bengaluru residents alongside government reports and newspaper data, this paper finds that the answer is complicated. Plastic waste did fall after the ban came into effect, larger retailers have largely complied. But in local markets and among lower-income vendors, little has changed. Alternatives are too expensive, enforcement is inconsistent, and awareness of what is actually banned remains patchy. The result is a ban that works well for some and barely at all for others.

title: Labor Market Power over the Business Cycle

detail.title: Labor Market Power over the Business Cycle
detail.abstract: I study the cyclicality of labor market concentration and wage markdowns. Using linked employer-employee data from Portugal, I document novel facts that existing models cannot explain: (a) local labor market concentration is countercyclical; (b) wages move closer to marginal revenue products of labor during booms; and (c) markdown dispersion across producers rises in recessions. Using an IV strategy, I show that cyclical concentration accounts for 7 percent of procyclical firm pay. To explain these patterns, I develop an oligopsony model with differentiated jobs, strategic hiring, and endogenous business entry. The model links cyclical concentration to earning dynamics and labor misallocation.

title: Can Financial News Sentiment Predict Next-Day Price Movement Direction For NSE-Listed Large-Cap Stocks?
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Can Financial News Sentiment Predict Next-Day Price Movement Direction For NSE-Listed Large-Cap Stocks?
detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether financial news sentiment can predict the next-day price direction of largecap stocks listed on the National Stock Exchange of India (NSE). Using a five-year historical window from January 1, 2021, to December 31, 2025, we built an advanced natural language processing (NLP) pipeline to clean and analyze headlines from Business Standard. Headlines were normalized using Python's NLTK package under the Loughran-McDonald financial dictionary guidelines to preserve critical directional words. Sentiment scores were generated using FinBERT, a deep-learning AI transformer fine-tuned for corporate finance text. To eliminate forward-looking data leakage, any news published after the 03:30 PM IST NSE closing bell was algorithmically rolled into the next trading day, resulting in a clean dataset of 4,205 active daily records. Stationarity was confirmed across all 13 equities using the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test (𝑝 < 0.05). Bivariate Granger Causality tests revealed that news sentiment does not cause a global, uniform forecasting edge across all large-cap stocks, confirming the Semi-Strong Form of the Efficient Market Hypothesis for heavily traded assets like RELIANCE and HDFCBANK. However, a significant localized exception was discovered for SUNPHARMA (𝑝 = 0.01109), proving that technical sectors face an informational diffusion delay with an optimal lookback lag of 2 trading days. Finally, an out-of-sample Random Forest Classifier was trained using a chronological 80/20 train/test split. The machine learning model demonstrated strong predictive power on unseen 2025 data, peaking at a 60.00% directional accuracy for both HINDUNILVR and ULTRACEMCO, and a 55.56% accuracy with a 60.00% Precision Score for INFY. These findings provide clear evidence that text-driven trading signals can capture high-precision arbitrage windows in select sectors of emerging markets.

title: Information and Preferences in Shareholder Voting
affiliations: Rice University, Duke University- Fuqua School of Business and Duke University, Fuqua School of Business

detail.title: Information and Preferences in Shareholder Voting
detail.abstract: We develop a structural model of shareholder voting with incomplete information about proposal quality. We show that preferences and information are not separately identified from individual voting patterns alone: correlated information and strategic voting jointly determine the mapping from preferences to votes. Identification arises through cross-shareholder voting correlations and differential exposure to public information across investor types. Estimating the model on mutual fund voting, we recover institution-level information precision and information-corrected preference parameters. Despite higher support for management, blockholders' preferences are close to those of dispersed shareholders. Equalizing information across investor types has a larger effect on voting than equalizing preferences.

detail.abstract: Drought is a major threat for pastoralists in developing countries who depend on grazingbased livestock rearing. In the absence of adequate financial risk management tools, extreme dry spells expose livestock-dependent households to the risk of falling into a poverty trap. Option contracts that create the right to purchase livestock feed at a predetermined price could serve to both mitigate that risk and smooth volatility in feed and livestock markets that are destabilized when drought occurs. We present a theoretical framework for valuing such option contracts on both the individual buyer (pastoralist) and individual seller (feed provider) sides. We use a numerical simulation model based on data from the Sahelian region of West Africa to assess the potential viability of such option contracts and examine their impact on feed and livestock price volatility. That numerical analysis indicates that establishing option contracts is feasible in principle, that option contracts could increase pastoralists' drought-year incomes by as much as 17% at a cost of a 5% reduction in normalyear incomes, and that option contracts help stabilize feed and livestock markets. We discuss practical considerations affecting implementation of these contracts.

detail.abstract: Women across the globe are always trying to balance their work and personal life. Whether engaged in domestic chores alone or saddled with the 'double burden' of productive work and household work, they frequently suffer from time poverty and are permanently engaged in a futile effort to balance 'work' and life. In this paper we explore the issue of work life balance among females in India using Time Use Survey data. We devise a Work/Life Balance index and estimate the incidence and magnitude of work life (im)balance using this index. We also try to identify drivers of work life balance from binary and multinomial logistic regressions.

title: Against the Duplicity Thesis: Pakistan Army as Ideological Defender in the American War on Terror

detail.title: Against the Duplicity Thesis: Pakistan Army as Ideological Defender in the American War on Terror
detail.abstract:
The dominant academic consensus characterizes Pakistan's conduct during the American War on Terror as institutionalized duplicity — simultaneously fighting and sheltering the Taliban while extracting American funding. This paper argues that the "duplicity thesis" fundamentally misreads the institutional logic of the Pakistan Army.

Drawing on declassified U.S. government records, GAO audit data, IMF documentation, and published military doctrine studies, the paper advances three arguments. First, Pakistan's ideological deformation was externally produced: the Treaty of Darin (1915) created the Saudi state, whose petrodollar revenues subsequently funded Deobandi-Wahhabi madrassa expansion across Pakistan — a British imperial act, not a Pakistani civilizational choice. Second, the Army's institutional identity is rooted in Iqbal's Persian-Sufi synthesis and is demonstrably Barelvi-compatible; Zia ul-Haq's Deobandization was a Cold War patronage rupture, not the institutional norm. Third, Pervez Musharraf extracted $23 billion in economic relief — including $5.56 billion in Coalition Support Funds (81% of the global program), $12.5 billion in Paris Club debt restructuring, and nuclear sanctions lifted within 36 days of 9/11 — while simultaneously dismantling Deobandi extremist organizations and culminating in the Lal Masjid operation of July 2007. The actual vector of Saudi ideological capture in Pakistan has been civilian politicians, most notably Nawaz Sharif, whose Saudi nexus is documented in the Panama Papers. Reframing the Army as a civilizational defender restores analytical clarity to a debate paralyzed by the duplicity thesis.

title: AI-powered Educational Technologies and Student Learning Outcomes in Universities
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: AI-powered Educational Technologies and Student Learning Outcomes in Universities
detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered educational technologies have increasingly transformed university education by improving instructional delivery, learning personalization, academic assessment, and student engagement. Universities worldwide are adopting intelligent educational systems such as adaptive learning platforms, intelligent tutoring systems, predictive learning analytics, automated assessment tools, and generative AI applications to strengthen teaching effectiveness and improve student learning outcomes. These technologies support personalized educational pathways by analyzing student performance, monitoring engagement patterns, and providing individualized academic feedback capable of enhancing learner performance and retention. This study examines the influence of AI-powered educational technologies on student learning outcomes in universities through a narrative review of scholarly literature. The article explores how intelligent educational systems contribute to academic achievement, learning engagement, motivation, self-regulated learning, retention, and educational accessibility while also evaluating challenges affecting implementation effectiveness. Findings indicate that AIdriven educational technologies improve learning efficiency through adaptive instructional systems, real-time performance monitoring, automated academic support, and predictive intervention strategies designed to assist struggling learners. Furthermore, intelligent learning environments enhance educational responsiveness by enabling educators to make evidence-based instructional decisions that support improved student outcomes. However, concerns relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, technological inequality, digital literacy, institutional preparedness, and excessive dependence on intelligent systems remain significant barriers to sustainable implementation. The study concludes that AI-powered educational technologies have substantial potential to improve university student learning outcomes, but successful implementation requires ethical governance, institutional readiness, faculty competence, and inclusive access to digital learning resources.

detail.title: Ukraineʼs Electricity Sector: Urgency and Resilience in a Time of War
detail.abstract: Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s electricity sector have made power supply a core battlefield of the war. This paper argues that Ukraine’s centralized, Soviet-legacy grid is strategically vulnerable and must shift rapidly toward distributed, dispatchable generation. Diesel generators can help address immediate winter humanitarian needs, but gas-fired turbines, piston engines, and cogeneration units offer a more scalable, lower-cost bridge to resilience. Dispersed 1–50 MW assets would also raise Russia’s cost per megawatt destroyed, especially if hardened and insured. War-risk insurance, sovereign guarantees, and allied financing can unlock private capital and make Ukraine’s electricity reconstruction a model for wartime resilience.

title: Transit and Logistics Potential of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic: Strategic Development Prospects in the Context of Regional Connectivity

detail.title: Transit and Logistics Potential of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic: Strategic Development Prospects in the Context of Regional Connectivity
detail.abstract: The Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic possesses significant transit and logistics potential due to its strategic geographical location at the intersection of regional transportation routes connecting the South Caucasus, Türkiye, and Central Asia. Recent geopolitical and economic transformations in Eurasia, particularly the emergence of the Zangezur Corridor and the increasing importance of the Middle Corridor, have strengthened the region's role in international freight transportation and multimodal logistics systems. This study examines the current state of Nakhchivan's transport infrastructure, crossborder trade opportunities, and logistics capabilities while evaluating future development perspectives within regional integration processes. The research also analyzes the impact of digital transformation, smart logistics ecosystems, and modern customs technologies on the efficiency of transit operations. Particular attention is devoted to transport diversification, infrastructure modernization, and the enhancement of regional connectivity through railway and highway projects. The article employs comparative analysis, statistical evaluation, and theoretical approaches based on regional economic development concepts. The findings indicate that Nakhchivan has the potential to become an important logistics hub in the South Caucasus by strengthening trade flows, improving transit efficiency, and integrating into international transport corridors. Furthermore, sustainable investments, institutional reforms, and digital logistics solutions are identified as essential factors for long-term competitiveness and economic resilience in the region.

ARIN serves institutional risk decision workflows for Chief Risk Officer buyers in banks, asset managers, insurers, and sovereign funds. The shared mathematical kernel performs the foundational risk-computation layer in both applications. 
We construct a rolling-window backtest framework with N = 500 forecast initiations on each of 180-day and 360-day horizons, using an 11-year price panel of 463 Fortune 500 names (2 January 2015 through 1 June 2026; 2,869 trading days), with regime tagging across bull, normal, bear, and high-volatility periods. detail.abstract: Horizontal mobilization dynamics prove more resilient against repression, but they complicate efficient organization and the projection of a coherent public image. Tensions between spontaneity and innovation, and the need for reliable arrangements and sustainable infrastructure are particularly evident within protest camps. This article examines these tensions by exploring the socio-spatial arrangements of Tripoli's Thawra protests during Lebanon's revolutionary uprising of 2019/2020. Leveraging 49 semi-structured interviews alongside a dozen structured conversations with activists and protest participants, we argue that the infrastructural complexity, cultural diversity, and tactical variety of protest camps necessitate a high degree of flexibility by protesters who must balance internal relations and their external engagement with the larger revolutionary theatre. To capture this dual struggle, we conceptualize protest camps as arenas within arenas, whose spaces serve as sites of negotiation of norms, practices and hierarchies. We illustrate this concept through the case of Tripoli, where the square, the island of tents, and the barricades emerged as three central subarenas to calibrate the relationships of camp participants, in turn, shaping the specific character of Tripoli as a distinct contentious arena within the larger revolutionary theatre.

title: On the Origins of the Multinational Premium
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and Boston University

detail.title: On the Origins of the Multinational Premium
detail.abstract:
We study the relationship between management, multinational expansion, and risk premia. We document two facts: firms run by better managers are more likely to become multinationals (MNEs), and risk premia are higher for current and future MNEs than for firms that remain exclusively domestic. We develop a model in which endogenous matching between heterogeneous firms and managers jointly determines selection into foreign direct investment (FDI) and risk premia. Quantitatively, we use the model to examine how corporate taxation and distortions in the market for managerial talent affect multinational activity, firm risk exposure, and financial market outcomes.

title: What Happens to Contractors After States Ban Affirmative Action?
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: What Happens to Contractors After States Ban Affirmative Action?
detail.abstract:
Using restricted Census business records, I explore how banning affirmative action in state contracting affects minority- and women-owned business enterprises (MWBEs). I find that ending affirmative action led MWBE contractors to gradually downsize, with the most pronounced reductions in force experienced by Black-owned businesses and larger MWBEs. Despite these workforce changes, existing MWBEs were no more likely to shut down than other businesses. New MWBEs were relatively less common after a state's ban, highlighting how bans can shift the demographic composition of new contractors. A calibrated model suggests bans are equivalent to considerable reductions in MWBE productivity and scrap values.

title: Shaping Major Choice: The Role of High School Counselors
affiliations: Texas A&M University, Texas A&M University - Department of Economics and Texas A&M University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Shaping Major Choice: The Role of High School Counselors
detail.abstract:
Existing studies show that high school counselors can significantly influence students' graduation rates and college enrollment; less is known about their ability to direct students toward particular fields of study. We evaluate an information intervention aimed at increasing counselors' awareness of economics, a major often associated with misconceptions about its content and career opportunities, and characterized by substantial under-representation of women and racial and ethnic minorities. Counselors from randomly selected Texas high schools were invited to participate in a one-day information workshop on the economics major. We evaluate the impact of the intervention on students' major preferences and outcomes using application and admissions data from a large public university attended by many graduates from the treatment schools, as well as enrollment and course-taking records from the Texas Education Research Center. The intervention led to substantial increases in interest in economics at the college application stage, particularly among high-achieving women, but did not lead to significant changes in college major outcomes. We conclude that high school counselors can play an important role in shaping students' field-of-study preferences, but translating preferences into enrollment requires additional exposure and reinforcement.

title: Paying for Quality vs. Paying for Rank: When Purifying a Metric Backfires
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management and

detail.title: Paying for Quality vs. Paying for Rank: When Purifying a Metric Backfires
detail.abstract:
Matching markets allocate scarce opportunities using performance metrics that agents can game. When does making a metric less gameable actually reduce gaming? We show that the answer hinges on how the market converts evaluations into stakes. Where evaluations assign prices — wages, credit terms, score-indexed payments — partially purifying the metric raises gaming precisely when gameable variation dominates it: the market's trust in the metric then rises faster than its exposure to gaming falls. By contrast, where evaluations assign positions — fixed seats allocated by rank — purification never backfires: ranking cancels trust from the incentive, leaving a rank price that deflates with the metric's dispersion, so mean gaming falls monotonically. We solve both markets in closed form under a first-order equilibrium concept; transfers microfound the first regime, rank tournaments the second. A prize-curvature index then determines when gaming improves rather than harms sorting, and when perfecting the metric is itself sorting-suboptimal.

We use thermal inversions, weather phenomena that trap pollutants, as an instrumental variable for pollution. A one-unit increase in the county-week average ambient particulate pollution level decreases attendance by around 2 percentage points. Effects seem to be larger for racial minorities and for children with working parents.

title: Identity Uncertainty
affiliations: University of California, Davis, Duke University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: Identity Uncertainty
detail.abstract:
Many group identities that influence economic behavior are imperfectly observed. Individuals and institutions often conceal identity markers to limit discrimination. Yet concealment also creates uncertainty about group membership, hampering coordination in social interaction. To study this tradeoff, we paired high- and low-caste men for collaborative data entry work in North India. We randomly assigned each mixed-caste pair to either be: (i) introduced by full names, making caste common knowledge; (ii) introduced by first names only, making caste disclosure a choice; or (iii) instructed not to disclose caste. The two concealment conditions substantially reduce the accuracy of beliefs about a partner’s caste and confidence in those beliefs. They also weaken workplace relations, lowering trust, willingness to interact, and perceived productivity—consistent with identity helping structure social coordination. Evidence on mechanisms shows that identity concealment inhibits authentic interaction, making workers less able to express their “true selves,” while certainty about a partner’s identity is associated with stronger workplace ties. Concealment leaves a sizable caste disparity in higher-status role assignment intact, implying minimal impacts on discrimination. We conclude that where group identities are socially entrenched, reducing their legibility may undermine intergroup relations.

title: Misleading Estimates from Nonlinear Models with a Binary Outcome
affiliations: University of Chicago, University of Chicago and University of Virginia

detail.title: Misleading Estimates from Nonlinear Models with a Binary Outcome
detail.abstract:
When estimating nonlinear models for binary outcomes, such as probit and logit models, researchers often rely on average partial effects (APEs) to summarize the effect of a regressor. Because the marginal effect of a variable in these models depends on the values of all other variables, the value of an APE hinges on the portion of the sample used for the calculations. When averaged over parts of the sample drawn from a subpopulation not used to define the object of interest, the APE may be misleading. This paper highlights common situations, such as differences-in-means with a secondary group and difference-in-differences designs, where APEs calculated for the full sample deviate from marginal effects for the appropriate part of the sample. We propose a simple and costless solution in specific cases and demonstrate through simulations that recalculating APEs over the appropriate subsample yields unbiased results. Reexamining published results from multiple papers, we find statistically significant discrepancies between the reported estimates and the appropriately calculated APEs.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether the inter-industry wage differentials in India's organised manufacturing sector reflect genuine structural features of industry identity or are merely epiphenomena of observable differences in labour productivity and capital intensity. Using a balanced panel of 25 NIC two-digit industry groups drawn from the Annual Survey of Industries over the period 1980-2022, the convergence analysis reveals a structurally entrenched wage hierarchy. This persistence in wage differences is inconsistent with a purely competitive labour market in which transitory shocks determine relative wages. The fixed effects estimates identify a significant, positive within-industry elasticity of wages with respect to labour productivity and a smaller but statistically robust elasticity with respect to the capitallabour ratio. However, the most important point relating to the significance of the coefficients of the industry dummies is noteworthy. It reflects the composite influence of unobserved workforce quality, product market concentration, union density, establishment size, and the historical path dependence of industry-specific wage norms and many other unobservable characteristics. Facilitating the rapid growth of high wage industries and the movement of workers to these industries could raise economy-wide average wages and reduce the degree of wage inequality.

Over the longer term, treatment students were 3.2 percentage points more likely to enter elite high schools and 2.5 percentage points less likely to miss the entrance exam. We trace these gains to improved self-beliefs and a restructuring of classroom friendship networks that reduced academic homophily, revealing a social channel of cross-productivity: non-cognitive investments can reshape peer relationships to improve academic outcomes.

title: Climate and Prehistoric Migration

detail.title: Climate and Prehistoric Migration
detail.abstract:
What factors drove human migration before modern states, markets, and borders? We develop a sorting framework in which climate-specific subsistence knowledge depreciates with ecological distance. To test this, we use ancient DNA identity-by-descent segments to construct bilateral migration flows across Western Eurasia over the last 10,000 years. We document three main findings. First, migration flows decline with differences in growing degree days, precipitation, and soil characteristics between origins and destinations. Second, the binding factor varies across subsistence systems: farmers exhibit strong thermal and soil matching, while pastoralists match most strongly on precipitation. Third, periods of warming increase farmer expansion while cooling increases pastoral expansion in patterns that recover known archaeological migration episodes. Migration also acts as a margin of climate adaptation: populations exposed to temperature change move to destinations that partly offset the shift.

title: The Search Costs of Inflation in the Labor Market
affiliations: Duke University, University of Notre Dame - Department of Economics and

detail.title: The Search Costs of Inflation in the Labor Market
detail.abstract:
This paper studies the effect of unanticipated inflation in the labor market. When wages are contracted in nominal terms, inflation reduces real wages, leading workers to intensify on-the-job search to obtain wage-adjusting outside offers. Both the search effort and the resulting job mobility are costly, yet that same mobility raises output by moving workers toward more productive matches. To quantify these costs and benefits, we extend the canonical job ladder of Postel-Vinay and Robin (2002) to a nominal environment with privately chosen search effort, and calibrate it to standard moments from the pre-pandemic US labor market. A one-time inflation shock scaled to the COVID episode generates an average welfare loss of 0.44% of consumption, with workers at the top of the wage distribution bearing losses over six times those at the bottom. Once the offsetting transfer of surplus to firms and productivity gains from reallocation are accounted for, the net aggregate cost is close to zero. Second, inflation volatility imposes asymmetric costs: worker welfare is approximately invariant to the volatility regime because firms compensate workers for expected search costs at hiring, but social welfare declines meaningfully because the resource cost of search effort is not undone by compensation. This second finding identifies a distinct, labor-market source of welfare costs from inflation volatility, complementing the price-dispersion costs emphasized in the New Keynesian literature.

Can AI improve workplace outcomes for workers with disabilities? We examine the relative performance of deaf or hard of hearing (DHH) workers on one of China's largest food-delivery platforms. AI eliminates one-third of the disability hourly pay gap and significantly increases the profitability of DHH workers for the platform.

detail.title: The Golden Constant as the User Interface of Authority Gold, Governance Costs, and the Natural Grace Period Hypothesis

detail.abstract: Why can human societies maintain order without rulers constantly exercising violence, and without explaining complex doctrines or narratives from scratch in each individual situation? This paper addresses that question by redefining authority as a governance device that simultaneously reduces the costs of violence and meaning. Violence requires constant surveillance and repression; meaning requires long-term education and shared context. Authority is a cognitive shortcut that economizes these two high-cost devices and elicits obedience by merely being there. Authority does not, however, eliminate the need for education in meaning. Rather, it compresses meanings accumulated through education, ritual, and repetition into symbolic media such as flags, crowns, temples, currency, and logos, allowing them to operate instantly in specific situations. This paper conceptualizes that function of authority as a user interface (UI) that converts information between rulers and the ruled. The UI of authority recalls the possibility of violence without actual violence, and it makes the legitimacy of meaning intuitively available without lengthy explanation. The most successful historical medium of this interface was gold. Because gold does not corrode, shines distinctively, is scarce, and can be worked into symbolic forms, it visually implemented the permanence, sacredness, and uneven distribution of authority across cultural and linguistic boundaries. The originality of this paper lies in three claims. First, it defines authority not as ethical legitimacy but as an amplifying device that reduces the governance costs of violence and meaning. Second, it analyzes gold not as a mystical substance but as an efficient UI for visualizing authority. Third, it presents the Natural Grace Period hypothesis: the geological contingency of gold reserves may have simultaneously satisfied three conditions for civilization: scarcity sufficient to generate authority, abundance sufficient for monetary circulation, and persistence sufficient to bridge the transition from the gold standard to communication-and information-based trust. The subject of this paper, therefore, is not gold itself. Gold is the clearest case through which the universal function of authority can be illuminated. Gold receded from the institutional center in 1971, but authority did not end. Brands, legal authority, national symbols, and digital assets are all alternative answers to the same question: how can people be made to obey without continuous violence and without costly education? The Golden Constant is therefore a claim not only about the quantity of gold, but also about the structural constant that human societies continue to require authority.

title: Order as the Dependent Variable

detail.abstract: Why do revolutions launched in the name of freedom sometimes collapse into civil war? Why can authoritarian regimes that severely restrict freedom maintain a degree of stability? Why do crude narratives such as conspiracy theories provide psychological relief to people living under uncertainty? This paper reformulates political and social disorder not as a clash of values, ideals, or institutions, but as a problem of social dynamics in which order is treated as the dependent variable. The central hypothesis is simple: what human beings have most persistently sought is not freedom itself, but predictability about the future, and order is the state that emerges when such predictability is continuously supplied. This paper treats order not as a normatively desirable condition, but as a descriptive and operationally observable state. Order is defined as a dynamic state in which the freedom phases of multiple actors fluctuate, the desire energy generated by such fluctuations interferes across actors, and yet this interference is continuously converted and dissolved into predictable forms without escalating into destructive collision. Freedom is a foundational concept composed of self-determination and non-interference. Freedom phase refers to the condition in which freedom is actually realized within society. What directly destabilizes order is not freedom itself, but desire energy generated by the decline of freedom phase. The social mechanisms that convert interference among desire energies into predictable distributions of outcomes are called interference-processing devices. The term 'processing' has no moral meaning. It refers to the operation by which unresolved interference is channeled into procedures, norms, markets, religion, law, violence, narratives, or other forms that allow actors to foresee what is likely to happen next. The claim that violence may also function as the most primitive interference-processing device is not a normative justification of violence. It is a descriptive claim about the conditions under which violence supplies predictability and the costs through which it sustains order. The paper further distinguishes three types of predictability: behavioral predictability, rule-change predictability, and subjective predictability. This distinction enables authoritarianism, democracy, rule of law, religious society, populism, conspiracy theories, revolutions, and even individual long-term index investing to be analyzed within a single coordinate system. The argument also connects with Friston's Free Energy Principle and active inference, while shifting the focus from prediction-error minimization at the level of individual cognition and action to the social-level conversion of intersubjective interference into predictability by means of externalized institutional and symbolic devices. Through critical dialogue with Hobbes, Parsons, Fukuyama, Acemoglu and Robinson, North, Ostrom, Rawls, Habermas, and Friston, this paper argues that the central question is not which order is desirable, but under what conditions order arises, persists, and collapses. To make the framework falsifiable, the paper presents operational definitions of key variables and testable hypotheses.

title: The "Double Deprivation" Dilemma of Rural Children's Education and Its Solution-A Qualitative Analysis Based on Grounded Theory

detail.title: The "Double Deprivation" Dilemma of Rural Children's Education and Its Solution-A Qualitative Analysis Based on Grounded Theory
detail.abstract: The educational attainment of rural children is crucial for cultivating local talent and revitalizing rural communities. To explore the mechanisms behind rural children's educational access, this study employed grounded theory analysis to conduct three-level coding on interview data from 131 stakeholders in rural education in County A, Henan Province, China. The research reveals that rural children face systemic exclusion in education due to the combined effects of economic resources and cultural symbols, with "dual deprivation" leading to suboptimal educational outcomes. To address these challenges, a "material-cultural" dual compensation mechanism should be implemented. This involves institutional restructuring, school reforms, village revitalization, family support, and technological empowerment to build a multidimensional support system. Such measures will enhance the overall educational efficacy for rural children, providing developmental momentum for their growth, talent cultivation, and rural revitalization.

title: The Social Dynamics of Freedom Phase and Desire A Theory of Declining Predictability and Restoring Energy

detail.abstract: Existing theories have often treated desire as an impulse to be restrained, an object to be maximized as utility, or a psychological force to be governed. In contrast, this paper defines desire as restoring energy generated by the decline of a freedom phase, and models the process through which that energy is converted into order formation through the channels of the rule of law, markets, and social security. The paper rejects the binary opposition that treats freedom as good and desire as bad. It instead presents a sequential mechanism: decline of the freedom phase, emergence of desire, channel design, and order formation. This mechanism provides a theoretical perspective for explaining where social energy arises, under what conditions it destroys order, and under what conditions it generates order. From this perspective, desire is not a foreign substance that disturbs social order. Desire is both a signal that the freedom phase has declined and an energy source for reorganizing society. The problem is not the existence of desire, but the channel through which desire flows. The rule of law blocks destructive channels such as violence, fraud, and coercion. Markets provide channels through which desire is converted into value for others. Social security institutions can be understood as devices that reconnect desires that cannot access markets to a minimum level of predictability. In this paper, desire refers to restoring energy that arises when a gap emerges between a desirable state implicitly assumed by an agent and the actual state in which the agent is placed. Hunger for food, demand for stability caused by income insecurity, demand for autonomy against domination, and demands for reform caused by institutional distrust differ in content, but they can all be understood as recovery responses to a decline in the freedom phase. The paper defines freedom as a basic concept composed of self-determination and non-interference, and calls the stable condition in which that freedom actually holds in society a freedom phase. A freedom phase is a condition in which an agent can feel that one's actions lead to outcomes, that one is not suddenly obstructed by the arbitrariness of others, and that one can act tomorrow with a certain degree of outlook. The degree to which a freedom phase holds is therefore observed through predictability. This paper reformulates freedom and desire as variables for describing how behavioral energy arises in society, separating them from the vocabulary of moral judgment. Conventional theories of freedom have treated freedom as an ideal to be protected and desire as a disturbing factor to be controlled. Yet this opposition cannot adequately explain why human beings seek freedom while accepting institutions, why they often choose stability over higher payoff, and why strong behavioral energy emerges when predictability is lost.

title: Legendre Wavelet Collocation Method for Pricing European Options Under Jump Diffusion Models
affiliations: Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana and Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana

detail.title: Legendre Wavelet Collocation Method for Pricing European Options Under Jump Diffusion Models
detail.abstract: The option pricing theory, an important aspect of derivative market pricing, provides a means of estimating the fair value of an option that traders consider in their profit strategy. However, empirical option data often exhibit stylized characteristics such as significant jumps or outliers, heavy tails, and asymmetric properties that are incompatible with the Gaussian model. To address this issue, jump-diffusion processes governed by integro-differential equations(IDEs) are investigated, with the presence of jumps indicated by the non-local integral term. Since the involved IDEs for pricing financial options have no closed-form solutions, numerical methods are used, but they are often associated with complex and dense matrices, resulting in slow computation times. In this study, the researchers proposed the Legendre wavelet collocation method (LWCM), for approximating Merton’s IDE. The implementation of the LWCM reduced the complex problem into an algebraic system of equations. The method yields sparse matrices, which enable faster computation times, and demonstrates high-order convergence rates for discrete L2 and L∞ norms. The results suggest that the proposed LWCM is a simple yet effective method for accurately approximating Merton’s analytic solution.

title: Grand Unification: The Spiral of Fate and Freedom

detail.title: Grand Unification: The Spiral of Fate and Freedom
detail.abstract:
This study is a synthesis that recovers the Gray Zone series (Papers 1–4) into a single integ‐
rated structure. Its central claim is simple: the hidden spine running through Papers 1–4 is the spiral of
fate and freedom. Beginning from fate (the structural limit of cognition), passing through the cognition that gazes at that limit, traversing the Gray Zone that mediates opposition, arriving at the realization of
freedom, and that freedom in turn becoming the condition of a new fate—this cycle is the form of the entire series. The study formalizes this spiral as the schema 0↔1↔4↔∞ and recovers Paper 1 (mediation principle), Paper 2 (baryonic epistemic ceiling), Paper 3 (grand unified cosmology), and Paper 4 (AGI political economy) each as one moment of the spiral. As its own contribution, the study then structures—rather than newly discovers—the way the spiral is concretized in the AGI transition as three manifestations of the deprivation of freedom: political legitimacy, epistemic truth, and existential subjectivity (the three crises Paper 4 §2.7 had already diagnosed as irreducible to distribution). Jung's Unus Mundus gives an intellectual-historical name to this integrative horizon, but the study strictly restricts it to a normative-layer interpretive coordinate, not a law of nature. The final thesis is the study's own: fate and freedom are not two opposing worlds but a single process that is generated together within the Gray Zone.

title: The Political Economy of AGI Transition: Labor Displacement, Capital Concentration, and Gray-Zone Mediation

detail.title: The Political Economy of AGI Transition: Labor Displacement, Capital Concentration, and Gray-Zone Mediation
detail.abstract:
This study defines the social crisis of the AGI transition not as a single event but as the superposition of four analytically distinguishable moments: labor displacement and capital concentration (causal channels ① and ②, on one plane), cognitive limitation (③, an epistemic condition that runs through all three channels), and institutional lag (④, the normative environmental condition within which the channels operate). These four are not four terms of equal standing, and this asymmetry is made explicit in the body. The adversary is not AGI itself but an unmediated AGI transition. The study methodologically separates the decomposition of causes from the branching of outcomes; the latter is described conditionally by converging the behavioral combinations of three actors-capital, intelligentsia, and the state-onto four attractors of the dialectical quartet Thesis•Mediation•Antithesis•Synthesis (正•中•反•合). Three claims are advanced. First, a passive cash-transfer Universal Basic Income addresses income loss but not ownership concentration or access inequality, and is therefore insufficient as a transition mechanism on its own. Second, even when both the distributive and asset layers are mediated, three irreducible crises remain-legitimacy, truth, and subjecthood-and the Gray Zone is not a device that "solves" these three but a diagnosis that reveals them as objects of mediation. Third, at the distributive layer the Gray Zone offers one of the most coherent-though not the only-institutional candidates for an integrative transition, by way of equity-linked predistribution. This structure is projected onto asset markets as well: under an unmediated transition, assets linked to the means of production and assets dependent on aggregate demand diverge and then build co-collapse pressure (§2.6). The objective is not to abolish market capitalism but to stabilize, in advance, the social foundation on which market capitalism itself depends so that the AGI productivity shock does not destroy it. The prescription of this study is Keynesian transition stabilization, not a neo-Marxian theory of collapse.

title: Democratic Erosion and Banking System Fragility: A Unified Theory of Political Regime Dynamics, Institutional Deterioration, and Systemic Financial Risk

detail.title: Democratic Erosion and Banking System Fragility: A Unified Theory of Political Regime Dynamics, Institutional Deterioration, and Systemic Financial Risk
detail.abstract: Does political regime deterioration contribute to banking-system fragility? We study this question in a panel of 138 countries over 1975-2022 by combining the Laeven-Valencia systemic banking crisis database with the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index, the Polity5 composite, the Dincer-Eichengreen central bank independence index, and the standard Demirgüç-Kunt-Detragiache macro-financial controls. We estimate a rare-events panel logit with random effects, cubic time splines, and several complementary identification strategies (lag structure, instrumental variables, an event study around backsliding episodes, and two natural experiments). The associational evidence indicates that a one-standard-deviation decline in the V-Dem Liberal Democracy Index is associated with an increase of 8-14 percentage points in the five-year-ahead predicted probability of a systemic banking crisis, against a baseline crisis probability of 2.02 percent; sustained Polity5 backsliding exceeding two points over five years is associated with an additional 6-11 percentage points. Mechanism tests are consistent with three institutional channels (central bank independence erosion, connected lending expansion, and disclosure suppression), which jointly mediate approximately three-quarters of the cross-sectional association. A Political-Institutional Fragility Index constructed as the first principal component attains an out-of-sample AUROC of 0.84 on a 2015-2022 holdout. Because the data are observational, because reverse causality from financial distress to democratic erosion is documented in the literature, and because the institutional channel variables are measured with non-trivial error, we interpret the evidence as consistent with-but not definitive proof of-a partial causal effect of democratic erosion on banking fragility. We discuss conditions under which IMF Article IV consultations, FSAP stress tests, and Basel macroprudential rules may warrant consideration of political-institutional variables, while flagging the political-neutrality, sovereignty, and false-positive concerns that would attend implementation.

title: The AI Capital Expenditure Trap: Endogenous Disaster Risk, Mean-Field Investment Equilibria, and Sovereign Liability Transitions

detail.title: The AI Capital Expenditure Trap: Endogenous Disaster Risk, Mean-Field Investment Equilibria, and Sovereign Liability Transitions

detail.abstract: Existing models of rare disaster risk treat catastrophe arrival as exogenous or driven by macroeconomic fundamentals external to firm behavior, leaving unexplained the endogenous emergence of systemic risk from oligopolistic capital accumulation. We develop a continuoustime general equilibrium in which technology firms play a mean-field investment game whose Markov Perfect Equilibrium generates socially excessive, irreversible capital accumulation. The equilibrium aggregate capital stock endogenously raises the arrival intensity of a systemic write-down event-the "AI CapEx Trap"-which we price in equity cross-sections and sovereign credit markets. We identify this mechanism empirically using GPU supply-side disruptions as an instrument for technology investment timing, exploiting the fact that TSMC capacity constraints reflect fabrication decisions made 18-24 months in advance and are orthogonal to contemporaneous AI revenue expectations. We document that a one-standarddeviation GPU supply shock increases technology sector CapEx by 187 basis points relative to non-tech firms, that the technology-specific variance risk premium exceeds the broad market VRP by 42 basis points when the sector leverage indicator activates, and that the US sovereign CDS spread widens by 8.3 basis points in response to an identified tech CapEx shock, with the credible interval excluding zero through a horizon of six quarters. A structural VAR attributes 14% of the forecast error variance in US sovereign CDS spreads at the eight-quarter horizon to tech CapEx shocks. Counterfactual simulations calibrated to matched moments show that in a stagnation scenario with activated endogenous risk, the sovereign CDS spread rises by approximately 26 basis points-a magnitude comparable to the widening observed during the European sovereign debt crisis for peripheral economies. The Pigouvian investment tax that restores the social optimum ranges from 2.1% to 4.8% of CapEx depending on the parametric regime.

detail.abstract: Inspired by Adam Smith and Friedrich Hayek, many economists have postulated the existence of invisible forces that drive economic markets. These market forces interact in complex ways making it difficult to visualize or understand the interactions in every detail. Here I show how these forces can transcend a zero-sum game and become a win-win business interaction, thanks to emergent social synergies triggered by division of labor. Computer simulations with the model Sociodynamica show here the detailed dynamics underlying this phenomenon in a simple virtual economy. In these simulations, independent agents act in an economy exploiting and trading two different goods in a heterogeneous environment. All and each of the various forces and individuals were tracked continuously, allowing to unveil a synergistic effect on economic output produced by the division of labor between agents. Running simulations in a homogeneous environment, for example, eliminated all benefits of division of labor. The simulations showed that the synergies unleashed by division of labor arise if: Economies work in a heterogeneous environment; agents engage in complementary activities whose optimization processes diverge; agents have means to synchronize their activities. This insight, although trivial if viewed a posteriori, improve our understanding of the source and nature of synergies in real economic markets and might render economic and natural sciences more consilient.

title: Insurance with Multiple Actors
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Yale University and University of Florida

detail.title: Insurance with Multiple Actors
detail.abstract: We analyze how social-planner insurers split cost-sharing between consumers and firms (e.g. patients and doctors, or drivers and car mechanics). With no contracting frictions, firm cost-sharing can replace consumer cost-sharing other than “visit copays.” Optimal firm contracts depend on the marginal rate of substitution between consumer and firm cost-sharing. For Medicare physician services, paying physicians more up front but less as spending increases reduces risk for both patients and providers; in our calibration, net benefits are twice those from eliminating Medigap externality. For prescription drugs, a dollar of physician paperwork costs is 45–110 times more impactful than a dollar of consumer cost-sharing.

detail.abstract:
Research question. The post-2022 AI narrative pushed enterprise-software multiples down on the fear that generative AI would commoditise SaaS workflows. We ask whether the repricing reflected deterioration in business value or a blunt AI-disruption narrative applied across firms whose fundamentals were in fact diverging.

Method. We rebuild the opportunity set from financial statements, not from price action. After carving out 12 payments/fintech firms whose float economics differ from SaaS, the core sample contains 335 firms with usable 2023 and latest-2026 endpoints. The analysis then follows one chain: (1) test business reality, 

(2) estimate intrinsic value independently of price, 

(3) read current price in reverse through implied growth, 

(4) attach signed AI exposure, and (5) convert only the surviving evidence into a portfolio watchlist.

 Results. The evidence indicates a cohort-specific mispricing of growth expectations rather than a uniform market error. 

(1) Expectations gap. By reverse DCF, the repricing mis-set implied growth with opposite signs across cohorts: AI-native firms are priced for materially higher growth than they delivered (implied 43.6% versus realised 25.5%), whereas profitable workflow incumbents are priced for lower growth than they delivered (implied 8.6% versus realised 13.8%). 

(2) Conversion test. Firms with the highest AI salience did not convert it into superior economics: their gross-margin change is significantly worse than matched controls (difference-in-differences -2.7 pp, t = -2.87). 

(3) Fundamentals and level value. Over the period the 167 FCF-positive firms improved (median SBC-adjusted FCF margin 5.5% to 11.6%, ROIC 5.7% to 14.0%) while the 168 pre-FCF firms deteriorated (FCF margin -27.8% to -33.6%, median runway 0.97 years). On level value, broad SaaS is not cheap (median margin of safety -17.7% FCF-positive, -84.4% pre-FCF); the only cohort with a positive median margin of safety is the exposed-incumbent group (19 firms, median MoS 2.9%, 57.9% undervalued).

Implications. The output is a small, gated, reproducible watchlist of workflow incumbents whose prices imply impairment that the financial statements do not yet show. It is an ex-ante valuation gap, not demonstrated realised alpha: a point-in-time, sector-neutral implementation of the signal earns no significant factor-adjusted return over the sample (FF5+momentum alpha = -14.0%, t = -0.97), so the gap had not yet been harvested. The same signed-exposure framework can be reused for future narrative shocks.

title: Who Takes the Hit? The Uneven Impacts of Generative AI on Labor Demand across Countries
affiliations: , World Bank, World Bank and World Bank

detail.title: Who Takes the Hit? The Uneven Impacts of Generative AI on Labor Demand across Countries
detail.abstract: Has generative AI begun to displace workers globally, or only in high-income countries? This paper exploits the November 2022 release of ChatGPT as a technology shock and applies difference-indifferences and event study designs to 555 million Lightcast job postings spanning 84 countries from 2021Q1 to 2025Q2, comparing labor demand across occupations with high versus low AI-substitution vulnerability. In high-income countries, postings for above-median vulnerability occupations declined by 5.8 percent on average relative to less substitutable occupations-after controlling for GenAI exposure and monetary policy sensitivity-with effects intensifying over time. In middle-and low-income countries, the impact is much smaller and statistically insignificant. Crosscountry analysis suggests that certain channels may have driven this divergence: displacement is larger in higher-income countries and, conditional on GDP per capita, in countries with greater GenAI adoption, more years of schooling, stronger English proficiency, and greater specialization in digital services trade. Together, these findings suggest that limited AI adoption, the absence of complementary factors for adoption, and potentially less exposure to digital services trade have so far muted the labor displacement effects in middle-and low-income countries.

title: The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education
affiliations: Stockholm University, The University of Hong Kong - University of Hong Kong and University of Hong Kong

detail.title: The Generative AI Learning Penalty: Evidence from Chinese Secondary Education
detail.abstract: Using 30 months of panel data on 26,811 Chinese students in grades 7-12, we study how generative AI affects homework productivity and learning. The data combine monthly closed-book exams, high-school and college entrance exams, and homework scores and completion time across nine subjects. We exploit staggered AI adoption in a difference-in-differences design. AI adoption raises homework scores by 18% and reduces completion time by 30%, but lowers monthly exam scores by 20% within six months. High-stakes entrance-exam scores fall by 18 and 24%, with the full penalty emerging only after about two years. The losses are largest in social science subjects, followed by STEM and languages, and are especially large for junior students, high-achieving students, and boys. The learning losses are concentrated among roughly 80% of AI users whose behavior is consistent with homework outsourcing, as indicated by exceptionally short homework completion time coupled with high homework scores. AI users who maintain similar homework completion time as non-AI users experience small learning losses.

title: Forward Guidance: Opening the Black Box of the New Keynesian Model

detail.title: Forward Guidance: Opening the Black Box of the New Keynesian Model
detail.abstract: The forward-guidance puzzle refers to the implausibly large effects of anticipated future interest rate changes on current output and inflation, as predicted by standard New Keynesian models. We analyze the underlying nonlinear model both theoretically and numerically, tracking the full distribution of prices across firms. We show that large output expansions arise only under extreme and economically implausible circumstances: firms unable to reset prices must sell below marginal cost while meeting unbounded demand, thus accumulating arbitrarily large losses. The model also exhibits asymmetric effects across policy directions, with important implications for the economy at the zero lower bound. When non-reoptimizing firms can at least set prices equal to marginal cost, output and inflation remain bounded, though not all forward-guidance announcements are feasible in equilibrium. Our results show that the puzzle relies crucially on a rarely discussed microeconomic assumption, and clarify the limits of New Keynesian models in analyzing large or persistent monetary shocks.

title: Environmental Socialization, Infrastructure Familiarity, and Communication Accessibility among First-generation Immigrant Populations in Ontario Recycling Systems
affiliations: Faculty of Environmental and Urban Change, York University

detail.title: Environmental Socialization, Infrastructure Familiarity, and Communication Accessibility among First-generation Immigrant Populations in Ontario Recycling Systems
detail.abstract: Municipal recycling programs in Ontario face a persistent participation gap among first-generation immigrant households. This exploratory cross-sectional study examines recycling participation, attitudes, and behavioral drivers among 795 households across twelve ethnocultural groups in three Greater Toronto Area municipalities. Drawing on acculturation theory, the Theory of Planned Behavior, and social practice theory, we situate observed behavioral variation within broader socio-material and institutional processes rather than treating ethnocultural identity as an explanatory endpoint. First-generation status was recorded at the individual level; group-level proportions are reported. Multivariate OLS regression indicates that settlement stage is a significant negative predictor of recycling behavior (β =-0.38, p < 0.05) and infrastructure familiarity (β =-0.44, p < 0.05), but not of recycling attitudes (β =-0.12, p > 0.05). This attitudecontrol dissociation is the study's core finding. When infrastructure familiarity is entered directly as a structural covariate (Model C), the first-generation coefficient attenuates from-0.38 to-0.22, with adjusted R² improving from .18 to .27. Disaggregating recycling behavior into curbside and depot sub-constructs reveals that first-generation gaps are concentrated in high-effort depot behaviors (first-gen β =-0.48) rather than routine curbside participation (β =-0.19). An extended confounder model confirms that settlement duration and language proximity partially account for, but do not eliminate, the first-generation effect. Findings are exploratory and subject to convenience sampling and self-report constraints. They suggest that participation gaps may be more productively addressed through infrastructure familiarity interventions targeting depot behaviors than through motivational campaigns.

title: Shock Tree versus Markov Chain in the Life-cycle Income Fluctuation Model
affiliations: Virginia Commonwealth University (VCU)

detail.title: Shock Tree versus Markov Chain in the Life-cycle Income Fluctuation Model
detail.abstract: We study discretization of a unit-root income process. The macroeconomics literature typically discretizes the income state, whereas the asset pricing literature emphasizes discretization of income innovations. We consider a finite-horizon income fluctuation model and compare two discrete approximations-(i) a Rouwenhorst-type Markov chain and (ii) a recombining binomial shock tree-against a continuous-income benchmark. We find that the choice of discretization affects distributional outcomes. With a small number of states, the Rouwenhorst approximation understates dispersion in income and consumption and reduces wealth concentration. In contrast, the shock-tree discretization closely matches benchmark moments. Increasing the number of states in the Rouwenhorst approach improves its accuracy and leads to convergence toward the benchmark. These results suggest that, in unit-root settings, discretizing innovations can provide a more accurate approximation of income uncertainty while maintaining a small state space.

title: Optimal Capital Gains Tax as an Incentive Contract
affiliations: University of New South Wales (UNSW), UNSW Business School

detail.title: Optimal Capital Gains Tax as an Incentive Contract
detail.abstract: We recast optimal capital gains taxation as a moral-hazard problem: the government is a principal, the investor an agent whose unobservable investment-effort produces a noisy gain. The tax rate is the slope of a linear sharing rule. We distinguish revenue-maximizing from welfare-maximizing rates, reflecting the relative value of public-versus-private funds. Revenue-maximizing rates are high only under restrictive assumptions. Allowing for elastic investment, fiscal spillovers, growth effects, substitution toward lower-taxed assets or jurisdictions, and realization-based lock-in materially lowers optimal rates. Empirically grounded calibrations imply revenue-maximizing rates are low, often near zero, and below common statutory rates; welfare-maximizing rates are lower still.

detail.abstract: Semiconductor technologies have become central to artificial intelligence, digital infrastructures and geopolitical competition. Their development is shaped by technical innovation, industrial policy, supply-chain governance and strategic state interests. As sociotechnical artefacts, chips not only enable advanced computational services but also shape regulatory regimes, hierarchies of authority, and global digital autonomy. Raising demands for advanced services, automation, and large-scale AI models has produces a feedback loop in which societal needs and technical capabilities mutually reinforce one another. Semiconductor production is geographically concentrated, and this asymmetry embeds political authority within technological infrastructure, making governance dependent on export licensing, bilateral agreements, and trade restrictions that limit access and deepen global inequalities. Private firms, including fabless designers, foundries, and equipment suppliers are co-shapers of chip development trajectories. This paper examines how sociotechnical factors and state strategies together shaped semiconductor governance. Drawing on policy frameworks (U.S. export controls, EU Chips Act, India's Semiconductor Mission), trade governance instruments, and industry reports, it argues that global semiconductor regime shapes geopolitical, economic, and socio-ecological inequalities. The paper further contends that semiconductor policy in Asia should move towards ecosystem development through investment in workforce training, design capabilities, regional cooperation and technological resilience.

detail.abstract: As strategic competition between the United States and China intensifies, tensions in the Taiwan Strait are escalating. The wars in Ukraine (2022) and between Israel and Palestine (2023) have further heightened global uncertainty. The Council on Foreign Relations (CFR) has designated Taiwan as the most dangerous region since 2021. U.S. military, intelligence leaders, and academic experts have warned of potential military conflict over Taiwan by 2027, and numerous reports assume U.S. intervention in the event of a Chinese invasion. China has conducted four large-scale military exercises around the Taiwan Strait since the visit of U.S. House Speaker Nancy Pelosi during President Tsai Ing-wen’s administration (2016–2023) and following the inauguration of President Lai Ching-te (2024–present). The Trump administration’s second term further underscored China’s expanding influence and its ambitions regarding Taiwan in its Interim National Defense Strategic Guidance (INDSG) released in March 2025. Against this backdrop, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) strengthened pro-independence stance, increased U.S. legislative and military support, and China’s declaration of possible military unification have collectively exacerbated political and diplomatic instability among the United States, China, and Taiwan. In particular, Taiwan’s geostrategic value—bolstered by its advanced semiconductor technology—is gaining prominence, further intensifying U.S.-China rivalry. (The rest omitted.)

title: Entrepreneurship in Quasi-Markets: An Institutional Analysis
affiliations: HFI, Institute of Retail Economics and Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN)

detail.title: Entrepreneurship in Quasi-Markets: An Institutional Analysis

declarations.funderStatement: Magnus Henrekson acknowledges financial support from Jan Wallanders och Tom Hedelius stiftelse (P2023- 0186) and from the Kamprad Family Foundation for Entrepreneurship, Research & Charity (P20220048).

publicationDetails.journalName: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: To bolster entrepreneurship and innovation in welfare service provision, numerous countries have established quasi-markets. Yet, the actual benefits from these reforms have often been modest. We posit that quasi-markets can realize their potential only within the appropriate institutional framework, which highlights the need for studies in the field of institutional economics that identify how best to regulate quasi-markets so that they deliver in line with these expectations. While competition and the presence of forprofit actors are necessary conditions for quasi-market improvements, they alone are insufficient. We illustrate this point by showing how the three leading entrepreneurship conceptions-Knightian, Kirznerian, and Schumpeterian-risk falling short of their potential in typical quasi-market setups. Most importantly, we identify the need for a set of complementary institutions that are epistemic in nature. Such reforms should help bolster (Knightian, Kirznerian, and Schumpeterian) quasi-market entrepreneurship and help users construct the requisite knowledge to make informed choices.

title: Do Not Drain The Swamp! Populism, Bureaucracy and Economic Performance
affiliations: Bocconi University, University of Cambridge, Faculty of Economics, Students and King’s College London

detail.title: Do Not Drain The Swamp! Populism, Bureaucracy and Economic Performance

publicationDetails.journalName: BAFFI Centre on Economics, Finance & Regulation Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Populist leaders often campaign against bureaucratic constraints, yet their economic performance may depend on the very institutional environment they inherit. We examine whether bureaucracy moderates the economic costs of populism using two complementary settings: crosscountry synthetic-control evidence and a U.S. state-year panel spanning 1929-2023. The crosscountry analysis offers suggestive evidence that the output decline following populist takeovers is attenuated in countries with stronger pre-existing bureaucratic institutions, particularly where bureaucracies are more independent. The U.S. state analysis provides sharper, within-country evidence. Leveraging LLM estimates of gubernatorial populism derived from State of the State speeches, we find that populist governors are associated with significantly lower per-capita income in states lacking an independent civil service, while no comparable penalty emerges-and the association is more than offset-where such protections are in force. Heterogeneity-robust event-study estimates point in the same direction, with the post-entry income decline concentrated in states without civil-service reform. Together, the evidence is consistent with independent bureaucracies acting as a partial buffer against the economic costs of populist governance: the "swamp" appears to dampen the damage populism would otherwise cause. * We wish to thank seminar participants in Cambridge for useful comments and Bocconi University and the Janeway Institute for financial support. The usual disclaimer applies.
