detail.abstract: This report summarizes and evaluates responses to a 2026 survey on the role of currency misvaluation in corporate decision-making and currency risk management. The survey’s most significant finding is that of the companies providing substantive responses, 71% discuss or consider currency misvaluation in long-term strategic planning, including 48% that specifically incorporate currency misvaluation into capital investment, financing, or capital allocation decisions. The survey also found that cash flow predictability and the “cost of hedging” are important considerations in short-term hedging decisions, but currency misvaluation is not.

title: Enabling Open Finance in EMDEs Incentives, Liability, and Performance Measurement
affiliations: , , University of Cambridge, Judge Business School, Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Students, , Bank for International Settlements, affiliation not provided to SSRN, , , BIS Innovation Hub, Bank for International Settlements (BIS), , Bank for International Settlements (BIS), and Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance, Cambridge Judge Business School, University of Cambridge

detail.title: Enabling Open Finance in EMDEs Incentives, Liability, and Performance Measurement

publicationDetails.detailsText: Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance Research Paper No.68
publicationDetails.journalName: Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAF) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
This report examines the key enablers that may support Open Finance ecosystems in delivering economic and social value in Emerging Markets and Developing Economies (EMDEs). Building on previous CCAF research into the State of Open Banking and Open Finance, both globally and in the Asia Pacific (APAC) region, it moves from the analysis of adoption and regulatory design to the ex-ante and ex-post conditions that may support long-term ecosystem viability. The report covers nine EMDEs: Brazil, Egypt, Ghana, India, Indonesia, Nigeria, the Philippines, Saudi Arabia, and South Africa. These countries represent different stages of Open Finance development, ranging from operational ecosystems with measurable adoption outcomes to countries where foundational design choices remain under active deliberation. The intention is to offer insights for regulators across all stages of implementation, drawing on 33 semi-structured interviews across 11 countries, complemented by a desk-based review of legislation, ecosystem dashboards, and published data. A cross-cutting observation underpinning the analysis is that Open Finance does not operate in a vacuum. Its design and performance are intrinsically linked to the broader financial services market, the wider regulatory environment and, increasingly, to developments outside financial services, including digital identity, BigTech, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and cross-sector data sharing.

This means that EMDE regulators may not be able to simply replicate an approach that has been successful elsewhere without accounting for these dependencies. Against this backdrop, this report's central contribution is a framework organised around three interlinked pillars: incentives, liability, and performance measurement. The framework's premise is that the three pillars reinforce one another, so that gaps in one can be at least partially offset by another. This interdependence can allow regulators to assess tradeoffs, sequence priorities, and identify which pillar most needs strengthening at a given stage. It is particularly relevant for EMDE regulators operating under institutional and resource constraints, where progress may need to be sequenced and rebalanced over time rather than pursued simultaneously from the outset.

The implications of this broader ecosystem dependence differ across each pillar. For incentives, it suggests that design may need to reflect local market structure, including who holds the most relevant data and whether mandates can realistically reach them. For liability, it suggests that Open Finance frameworks tend to build on top of existing legal architecture and dispute resolution systems, rather than replacing them. For performance measurement, the overlap between Open Finance, technological innovation, and financial innovation can make it harder to isolate the impact of Open Finance-specific interventions, and measurement design may therefore warrant careful consideration in light of these adjacencies. Given the small sample size and the nascent stage of several frameworks in scope, the findings across all three pillars are best interpreted as illustrative tendencies within the sample rather than cross-country conclusions.

title: Government Funding Costs Under Financial Repression
affiliations: London Business School, London Business School, Stanford Graduate School of Business and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Government Funding Costs Under Financial Repression
detail.abstract: We study the equilibrium effects of financial repression on government funding costs in an endowment economy with limited asset market participation. We show how a broad set of repression policies operates through a wedge in the Euler equation responsive to government size or by affecting fiscal redistribution between agents. Repression intensity is captured by a policy feedback rule that depends positively on net government spending. When fiscal policy is profligate and monetary policy accommodates, we show that such a repression policy raises bond values, reduces the inflationary cost of unfunded fiscal expansions, and lowers bond risk premia. Repression is not a free lunch for bondholders-they pay a lower inflation tax but also earn lower future real returns. When monetary policy does not accommodate fiscal policy, repression can provide stopgap funding for deficits, allowing the central bank to retain control over inflation while making government debt a hedge for fiscal inflation.

title: Equivalent Should Mean Equivalent: Closing the Loophole in State Generic Substitution Laws
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: Equivalent Should Mean Equivalent: Closing the Loophole in State Generic Substitution Laws
detail.abstract:
Pharmaceutical patent owners often seek to avoid the expiration of their patents by engaging in “product hopping” – swapping from one product to another just as the patent on the first product would expire, permitting generic competition. Product hopping has proven difficult to stop in practice because courts are reluctant to second-guess what can look like a genuine product improvement or the market’s reaction to it.

One type of product hop that should be simple to prevent involves minor or irrelevant changes to a product made solely for the purpose of preventing a generic drug from entering the market. Unfortunately, many state laws define equivalence differently than federal law does, creating a loophole in which a patent owner can change from one product to a (federally) equivalent product without doing any new testing, but doing so prevents generic substitution because the new product is not treated as equivalent in many states.

The problem here is simple: what the federal law treats as equivalent isn’t what most states define as equivalent for purposes of generic substitution laws. That creates a loophole that brand owners have been exploiting through product hopping.

My first solution to this problem is equally simple: Equivalent means equivalent. If the brand doesn’t need to do new testing because the FDA acknowledges that the new formulation is bioequivalent to the old one, so the switch doesn’t create safety or efficacy risks, pharmacists should be able to substitute the old drug for the new.

title: Taxable But Not Protected: Gendered Labor and the Limits of Work Law
affiliations: Pace University - School of Law

detail.title: Taxable But Not Protected: Gendered Labor and the Limits of Work Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: 61 Univ. of Richmond L. Rev. Online (2026)

detail.abstract:
Workers who create content on OnlyFans, participate in compensated egg transfers, or engage in sugar dating may be visible enough to be taxed without being visible enough to receive health insurance, retirement savings, paid leave, or unemployment protection. This Essay examines that gap between recognition and protection. Building on recent scholarship about preference-sensitive informality, the Essay argues that employee benefits law helps produce a form of "partial formality" in which labor is legally recognized for tax, income, or contractual purposes while remaining excluded from the social-insurance systems tied to formal employment. Through examples involving reproductive, affective, and sexualized labor performed disproportionately by women, the Essay shows how legal recognition often stops short of economic security. 

The Essay identifies this pattern as "recognition without protection." Rather than treating benefits exclusion as an accidental failure of regulation, it argues that contemporary labor markets increasingly separate legal visibility from long-term security for work performed by women and other minoritized people. The Essay concludes by cautioning that reforms focused solely on compliance or worker classification may increase legal visibility without delivering the protections that sustain work over time or provide long-term security for women and others.

title: Parameter Stability in Vasicek and CIR Short-Rate Models: A Cross-Country Analysis with Two Calibration Methods

detail.title: Parameter Stability in Vasicek and CIR Short-Rate Models: A Cross-Country Analysis with Two Calibration Methods

detail.abstract: This paper replicates and extends Zeytun and Gupta (2007), a comparative study of the Vasicek (1977) and Cox et al. (1985) one-factor short-rate models. Using 353 monthly observations of real government bond yields from Canada, the United States, and the Euro area spanning 1997 to 2026, we implement two calibration methodologies-direct bond price fitting (Method 1) and the Phillips and Yu (2005) two-stage estimator with Girsanov measure change (Method 2)-and provide the first direct comparison of their parameter stability properties. Our principal finding contradicts the original paper: across all three markets and both calibration methods, the CIR model produces more stable volatility parameter estimates than Vasicek, with the coefficient of variation for CIR σ ranging from 74 to 83 percent versus 158 to 251 percent for Vasicek. We attribute this to the Feller condition acting as an implicit regulariser in CIR calibration. We further document that Method 2 produces parameters 14.7 times more stable than Method 1 despite higher root-mean-squared pricing error, with direct implications for risk management applications. Extension to the full 1997-2026 dataset captures the zero lower bound era and the 2022-2024 rate hike cycle, regimes absent from the original study. Our results suggest that model selection in short-rate modelling should be evaluated separately for pricing and risk management objectives.

title: Synthetic Stablecoins and Financial Stability
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York and Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York

detail.title: Synthetic Stablecoins and Financial Stability

publicationDetails.journalName: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
On October 10, 2025, the announcement of a potential additional 100 percent tariff on Chinese goods drove risk-off moves across equities, Treasuries, credit spreads, and digital assets. Digital asset prices fell sharply, trading volumes surged, and liquidity vanished from key exchanges. In this post, we show how the price shock in digital assets was transmitted and amplified through a class of instruments called synthetic stablecoins—crypto assets whose structural design turned an external shock into a self-reinforcing deleveraging spiral within the crypto ecosystem.

title: The Textile Shock and the Family: Female-Intensive Trade Exposure and Birth Outcomes under NAFTA

detail.title: The Textile Shock and the Family: Female-Intensive Trade Exposure and Birth Outcomes under NAFTA
detail.abstract: Whether a trade shock reaches the health of the next generation depends on the gender of the jobs it destroys. NAFTA's deepest tariff cuts fell on textiles and apparel, an industry 62 percent female in 1990, a rare trade shock to women's jobs rather than men's. Using the restricted, county-identified universe of U.S. birth, fetal-death, and linked infant-death records and a recentered decomposition of the Hakobyan-McLaren county tariff shift-share into textile and durable-goods components, I show that NAFTA's birth-outcome effects load almost entirely on the female-intensive textile shock; a gendered first stage confirms it cut women's employment and left men's unchanged. Where the textile shock fell, low birth weight rose by 0.12 points and preterm birth by 0.16, fertility shifted toward prime ages (the rate at 25-29 rose by 1.8 per 1,000), and the unmarried-birth share rose by 0.83. Overall fertility and infant mortality did not move: the shock reshaped the composition and health of births, not their number or survival. The estimates survive shift-share randomization inference and multiple-testing correction. The health cost of trade adjustment falls on women and the next generation's births, not only on the displaced male workers the literature has counted.

title: Household Energy Transition and Fertility: Evidence from China's Clean Cooking Revolution
affiliations: Zhongnan University of Economics and Law and Jianghan University

detail.title: Household Energy Transition and Fertility: Evidence from China's Clean Cooking Revolution
detail.abstract: The transition from traditional solid fuels to clean cooking energy reshapes household time allocation and women's labor supply, with theoretically ambiguous implications for fertility. Health gains from reduced indoor air pollution may raise fertility; conversely, the opportunity cost channel, whereby time saved from fuel collection and cooking is redeployed into market work, may reduce it. Using seven waves of the China Family Panel Studies spanning 2010 to 2022, this paper provides the first systematic causal evidence on the fertility effects of household clean cooking adoption adopting instrument variable method. A one-unit improvement in cooking fuel cleanliness reduces cumulative fertility by approximately 0.12 children and lowers the probability of a new birth between survey waves by 1.8 percentage points; desired fertility also declines. Mechanism tests isolate two channels operating in opposite directions. Consistent with an opportunity cost channel, the fertility-suppressing effect is approximately 35 percent weaker for women who were already mothers at baseline, for whom the marginal opportunity cost of further childbearing is lower. Consistent with a health channel, the effect is approximately 39 percent weaker in households with infants under age five, whose vulnerability to indoor air pollution is greatest. The two channels are statistically indistinguishable in magnitude. Supporting evidence confirms that clean cooking significantly reduces women's housework time and increases both non-agricultural employment and household wage income. These findings document an unintended demographic consequence of household energy transition with implications for the coordinated governance of energy and population policies.

title: Weather Forecasts, Forecast Revisions, and Natural Gas Price Discovery
affiliations: University of Central Oklahoma, University of Central Oklahoma and University of Central Oklahoma

detail.title: Weather Forecasts, Forecast Revisions, and Natural Gas Price Discovery
detail.abstract: Previous studies examining the relationship between natural gas prices and market fundamentals have relied on realized weather conditions due to the lack of consistent weather forecast data. This study addresses this gap by employing a novel dataset of weather forecasts extending up to 14 days ahead. We investigate the roles of weather forecasts and forecast revisions in natural gas price discovery and compare their effects with those of realized weather. The results indicate that weather forecasts and forecast revisions, rather than realized weather conditions, exert significant effects on natural gas prices. We further document a pronounced asymmetry in market responses, with warmer-than-expected and colder-than-expected forecast revisions generating different price effects. In addition, we find that storage announcements significantly affect spot prices, but only on the following trading day. We also show that the impact of weather forecast revisions is unique to the natural gas market and is not observed in the crude oil market. These findings are robust across a range of alternative model specifications and robustness tests.This study provides direct evidence that natural gas prices respond primarily to weather expectations rather than realized weather outcomes, highlighting the importance of forward-looking information in energy price formation.

title: Reliable Energy Statistics for Successful Grand Transition
affiliations: Technical University of Sofia

detail.title: Reliable Energy Statistics for Successful Grand Transition
detail.abstract: AbstractThis paper outlines the lag in national and global energy statistics with respect to requirements of the Grand transition including:The conflict between modern decentralized energy systems vs centralized energy statistics;The inaccuracies because of lack of extracted energy and conversions’ entropy into obsolete national energy balances;The failures of Primary energy convention to comply with natural and legal laws;The contradiction between real and statistically presented nuclear energy;The misleading statistical assessment of energy import dependence;The untruths in proxy primarity of dispersed power sources: hydro, solar, wind etc. The insufficient engagement of the US Congress and the EU Parliament in the portliness of energy statistics is indicated.The paper proposes a new scope and toolkit of energy statistics.In conclusion, a hope is expressed that as part of the prerequisites for a successful Grand transition and further public sustainable development a multi-faceted process for a large-scale transition of energy statistics towards the creation of a comprehensive and reliable information system, encompassing all energy sources will be triggered. Such a system will feed data not only into the simple calculation of existing indicators, but also into all energy studies, e.g. Life Cycle Assessments, Energy Return of Investments, Exergy analysis, Climate changes analysis, etc.

title: The unanticipated emission reduction effect of fair competition policy: evidence from the cleanup of competitive tax incentives
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Central University of Finance and Economics and Beijing Wuzi University

detail.title: The unanticipated emission reduction effect of fair competition policy: evidence from the cleanup of competitive tax incentives
detail.abstract: Distortionary local tax incentives trigger less efficient interregional competition and resource misallocation, which solidify firms’ high-carbon production patterns and drive up overall carbon emissions. This paper first constructs a theoretical model to analyze how the cleanup of competitive tax incentives shapes firms’ carbon emission behavior. Leveraging China’s staggered rollout of the cleanup of competitive tax incentives since 2014 as a quasi-natural experiment, we then employ a staggered difference-in-differences (DID) framework and 2011-2021 listed firms data to explore the environmental effects of fair competition reform. The empirical results reveal that the cleanup of competitive tax incentives reduces corporate carbon emissions by an average of 0.84 million tons, and this finding remains robust after a series of robustness checks. The reform functions through optimizing production structures between inefficient and high-quality firms, stimulating technological innovation, and curbing rent-seeking behavior. Heterogeneity analyses show that the carbon reduction effect is more pronounced in regions with stronger government intervention, stricter environmental regulations, and lower economic growth targets, in industries with fierce competition and low tax contributions, and among zombie, subsidy-dependent, and strategic emerging firms. Overall, this study provides novel evidence that fairness-oriented market reforms deliver environmental co-benefits by enhancing resource allocation, offering critical insights for advancing low-carbon transitions.

detail.abstract:
Background: Cardiovascular diseases (CVD) are the leading cause of death worldwide, and their epidemiology is correlated with genetic predisposition, exposure to risk factors, sex, age, access to medical care, and other sociodemographic characteristics. Brazil is a developing country with a vast territory, which leads to structural inequalities. Estimates of CVD in Brazil, in its regions, and in its population are poorly evaluated and analysed.

Methods: We obtained CVD-related data from the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) and analysed mortality and morbidity from 1996 to 2023 by sex, race/ethnicity, age, and region. We calculated the risk of death from the most prevalent diseases, the average length of hospital stay, and the costs associated with heart transplantation.

Findings: In Brazil, acute myocardial infarction was the pathology that led to the highest number of deaths across all variables analysed during the evaluated period. Other CVD were also related to causes of death and morbidity, such as hypertensive diseases and heart failure.

Interpretation: Brazil presents a serious challenge to the public health system due to the high number of deaths and the progressive mortality rate. This study represents a fundamental contribution to the basis for formulating public health policies aimed at reducing the growing impact associated with these diseases.

detail.abstract:
Background: Evidence on the prevalence, severity, and geographic distribution of proteinuria during pregnancy is limited in mountainous and ethnically diverse regions. We assessed proteinuria and associated factors among pregnant women in Yunnan Province, China.

Methods: This retrospective cohort study analysed clinical records from health-care institutions across Yunnan Province. Among 268,012 records identified in 2020–25, 152,862 women without chronic kidney disease were included. Prevalence was estimated by severity. Associated factors were examined using mixed-effects ordinal logistic regression; restricted cubic splines assessed maternal age and pre-pregnancy body-mass index (BMI).

Findings: Mild proteinuria was present in 27.3% (95% CI 27.1–27.5), moderate proteinuria in 18.2% (18.0–18.4), and severe proteinuria in 2.2% (2.1–2.2) of women. Severe proteinuria increased with age, reaching 3.0% (2.8–3.2) among women aged 35 years or older, and varied geographically. After adjustment, greater severity was associated with older age, high personal medical burden, unstable employment or unemployment, some ethnic groups, residence in mountainous counties, smoking, dust or radioactive exposure, multiple pregnancy, hypertension, diabetes, and higher pre-pregnancy BMI. Hypertension had the strongest association (odds ratio 2.64, 95% CI 2.34–2.98).

Interpretation: Proteinuria was common and varied by severity, maternal age, and geography. Clinical and contextual characteristics associated with greater severity could inform antenatal monitoring and regional maternal health planning in diverse mountainous settings.

title: Aetiology-Specific Liver Cancer Burden in Sub-Saharan Africa, 1990–2023: A Global Burden of Disease 2023 Analysis

detail.title: Aetiology-Specific Liver Cancer Burden in Sub-Saharan Africa, 1990–2023: A Global Burden of Disease 2023 Analysis

detail.abstract:
Background: Liver cancer remains a leading cause of cancer mortality globally, with a disproportionate burden in low- and middle-income countries. In sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), the burden is heterogeneous across sub-regions and aetiologies, yet long-term analyses that are simultaneously aetiology-specific, sex-stratified, and sub-regionally resolved remain limited. This study assessed temporal trends and sub-regional heterogeneity in liver cancer burden across SSA from 1990 to 2023 using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2023 estimates.

Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of GBD 2023 data for SSA and its four sub-regions: Central, Eastern, Southern, and Western SSA. We extracted aetiology-specific estimates of liver cancer deaths, incident cases, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) attributable to hepatitis B virus (HBV), hepatitis C virus (HCV), alcohol use, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and other causes. Analyses were stratified by sex, year, and sub-region, with selected country-level estimates examined for HBV-attributable mortality. Both absolute numbers and age-standardised rates per 100,000 population were assessed. Temporal trends were quantified using estimated annual percentage change (EAPC). Analyses and visualisations were performed in R version 4.5.2.

Results: Central SSA carried the highest age-standardised liver cancer mortality burden throughout the study period. Western SSA experienced the steepest decline in age-standardised mortality over time. In 2023, HCV accounted for the largest share of liver cancer mortality in Central SSA, whereas HBV was the dominant aetiology in Western SSA. Eastern SSA showed a more balanced HBV–HCV profile, while Southern SSA demonstrated a mixed pattern with appreciable contributions from viral, alcohol-related, and metabolic causes. Male populations generally had higher aetiology-specific mortality rates than females across most strata, although the magnitude of the sex gap varied by aetiology and sub-region. At country level, the highest HBV-attributable mortality was observed in a small cluster of Western and Central SSA countries, including Guinea, Liberia, Mauritania, Chad, Gambia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Angola, and Gabon.

Conclusions: Liver cancer burden in SSA shows marked sub-regional and sex-specific heterogeneity. The predominance of HCV in Central SSA and HBV in Western SSA supports differentiated prevention strategies, including expanded access to HCV diagnosis and direct-acting antiviral therapy in Central SSA and strengthened HBV birth-dose vaccination in Western SSA. Additional attention to aflatoxin mitigation, HDV surveillance, alcohol control, and gender-responsive prevention strategies is warranted across the region.Keywords: Liver cancer; hepatocellular carcinoma; sub-Saharan Africa; hepatitis B virus; hepatitis C virus; Global Burden of Disease; age-standardised rates; sex disparities

detail.abstract: This paper examines how World Citi Colleges (WCC), a private higher education institution in the Philippines, can apply e-commerce principles-including online marketplaces, platform economies, and digital payment systems-to modernize its administrative and financial operations. Drawing on Management Information Systems (MIS) frameworks, the paper argues that transitioning from fragmented digital tools to a unified integrated platform would significantly improve enrollment processes, payment transactions, and overall service delivery. title: Reinforcement Learning-based Graph (De)Sampling for Social Recommendation

detail.title: Reinforcement Learning-based Graph (De)Sampling for Social Recommendation
detail.abstract: Social recommendations leverage users' social network information to facilitate product recommendations. To enhance recommendation effectiveness, desampling methods have been introduced to capture informative signals from social networks. This study proposes a novel reinforcement learning (RL)-based method for desampling-based recommendations. The exploration is directed by a reward function that prefers desampled networks with recommendation results that are similar to those of the original network. The reward function is calculated based on user and item representations generated from desampled social networks and user-item interaction networks with graph recommenders through neural networks. To improve RL efficiency, we introduced a simplified recommender into the framework. We also removed multiple links based on the user/item representations generated at the same stage. The proposed model significantly outperforms stateof-the-art graph desampling and RL-based methods for social recommendation.

title: Rethinking Privacy and Security in the Era of Decentralized and Agentic AI: A Systematic Literature Review
affiliations: Shahid Bahonar University of Kerman

detail.title: Rethinking Privacy and Security in the Era of Decentralized and Agentic AI: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: The rapid proliferation of decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) architecturesencompassing federated learning (FL), edge intelligence, peer-to-peer learning, and swarm intelligence systems-alongside the concurrent emergence of increasingly autonomous, Large Language Model (LLM)-based agentic AI, has fundamentally reshaped the privacy and security landscape. Traditional threat models and their defenses prove systematically inadequate in distributed environments where data remains partitioned across heterogeneous nodes and autonomous agents pursue long-horizon goals with minimal human oversight. This systematic literature review synthesizes 115 peer-reviewed studies published between 2017 and 2025 following a rigorous PRISMA 2020compliant methodology across seven major academic databases. We examine seven interconnected thematic pillars spanning federated learning security, agentic AI threat modeling, cryptographic foundations (MPC, HE, ZKP), post-quantum cryptography, blockchain governance, Edge AI and IoT security, Byzantine robustness, and privacy-preserving learning. Our synthesis identifies a fundamental three-way trilemma between privacy, security, and model utility as the central constraint on secure decentralized AI deployment. Key findings include the structural incompleteness of federated learning as a standalone privacy solution; novel agentic attack vectors including prompt injection, memory poisoning, and cascaded tool misuse that lack analogs in classical ML security; the prohibitive computational overhead of current cryptographic primitives; and the absence of standardized benchmarking frameworks. This review contributes a novel unified threat taxonomy across four planes, a comparative empirical analysis of privacy-preserving mechanisms, and a structured research roadmap for the six most critical open challenges.

title: Crowding Out the Crowd: How Intermediary Listing Volume Congests Lender Attention and Cannibalizes Its Own Loans in Digital Prosocial Lending

detail.title: Crowding Out the Crowd: How Intermediary Listing Volume Congests Lender Attention and Cannibalizes Its Own Loans in Digital Prosocial Lending
detail.abstract: Digital prosocial-lending platforms allocate capital through the attention of a finite crowd, yet the parties that decide how much loan content enters this shared information environment are not the lenders but the intermediaries that originate and list borrower loans. We study whether, how, and for whom an intermediary's own listing volume congests lender attention and slows, and jeopardizes, the funding of its own loans. Drawing on the loan-level records of 961,971 loans listed on Kiva between 2006 and 2025 by 430 intermediaries across 100 countries, we interpret the evidence through an attention-allocation account in which a finite, rivalrous pool of lender attention is divided across concurrently listed loans. We find that crowding a niche slows funding and lowers the probability that a loan funds at all, and that roughly three-quarters of the listings crowding a loan are supply its own intermediary chose to add (a median own-to-niche supply ratio of 0.80), consistent with a substantially self-imposed externality. Interestingly, the penalty is not uniform: it is buffered for loans that remain findable through distinctive narratives, amplified for loans with larger asks, and local, operating among same-niche substitutes and decaying as a listing surge clears. Identification rests on a shift-share instrument built from other intermediaries' supply and a within-partner surge event study with flat pre-trends. We reframe platform competition as a self-imposed, operational attention-congestion externality. We characterize lender attention as a finite, rivalrous resource that the crowd allocates within categories and reallocates only over time, with implications for platform governance and intermediary listing strategy. Theoretically, this study contributes to research on attention scarcity and platform competition in digital lending by identifying intermediary selfcannibalization as a self-imposed, supply-side congestion externality. Practically, it offers intermediaries and platform designers a concrete lever, the pace and niche composition of listings, for sustaining supply growth without eroding the attention each loan depends on.

title: Project CHRONOS: A Fully Homomorphic Ephemeral AI Agent with Provable Self Termination and Remote Verifiability
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Project CHRONOS: A Fully Homomorphic Ephemeral AI Agent with Provable Self Termination and Remote Verifiability
detail.abstract: We present CHRONOS, the first autonomous AI agent that simultaneously achieves plaintext blindness (all data is processed under fully homomorphic encryption without ever being exposed), cryptographically enforced time bound existence (the agent's own decryption key is locked behind a publicly verifiable proof of sequential work, rendering it inaccessible until a precise future moment), and remote verifiability of self destruction (a zero knowledge proof certifies that the key material has been irreversibly destroyed after mission completion). The agent's operational lifespan is governed by a "cryptographic fuse" constructed from a proof of sequential work (PoSW) whose computation time accurately matches the intended mission duration. A drand decentralized randomness beacon serves as a trusted time oracle to trigger the final key shredding. Crucially, the erasure proof is a non interactive zero knowledge argument (SNARK) that proves the correct execution of the entire self destruction sequence-including the PoSW solution, decryption of the private key, and subsequent memory zeroization-enabling any third party to cryptographically verify the agent's annihilation without trusting the agent or its hardware. We provide a complete system architecture, a formal security model with game based definitions and reductions to standard assumptions, and a proof of concept implementation using Zama's TFHE rs for encrypted inference, a Cohen Pietrzak PoSW implementation, and a Groth16 SNARK. Our benchmarks indicate that FHE inference on a small neural network (50 K parameters) completes in seconds, the PoSW background thread consumes negligible resources, and the erasure proof can be generated and verified in under three seconds. CHRONOS represents a fundamental advance in secure, disposable AI agents, with immediate applications in defense, intelligence, and high privacy environments.

title: On the Right to Obscurity
affiliations: Boston University School of Law and Rochester Institute of Technology - Department of Philosophy

detail.title: On the Right to Obscurity

publicationDetails.detailsText: Boston Univ. School of Law Research Paper
publicationDetails.journalName: Boston University School of Law Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
U.S. privacy law has largely failed to protect our most common yet also our most underappreciated form of privacy: the practical obscurity that allows us to live freely and with dignity. Obscurity, which is the state of protection that arises when personal information is difficult for some people to obtain or correctly interpret, provides the breathing room we need pursue self-development or establish healthy boundaries with others.

Around the world, there is tremendous anxiety about surveillance because new digital technologies and systems have drastically reduced obscurity. In this Essay, which reflects on Chinmayi Sharma, Thomas E. Kadri, and Sam Adler’s thoughtful and urgent article Brokering Safety, we argue in favor of a legally protected right to obscurity that is tied to human dignity and capabilities.

Appealing to this organizing principle can help lawmakers better mitigate the ongoing obscurity harms that people suffer every day. Indeed, a right to obscurity grounded in human dignity and capabilities can anchor a robust approach to surveillance reform that includes interventions, ranging from procedural rules to outright bans. Crucially, it can offer robust justification for bespoke interventions, such as one proposed in Brokering Safety, that protects our most ordinary and undervalued form of privacy.

title: AI Contagion in Social Networks
affiliations: and Université d'Évry

detail.title: AI Contagion in Social Networks
detail.abstract: We study how artificial intelligence (AI) interacts with social communication networks to shape the stability of collective knowledge. Agents exchange information through a network while receiving AIgenerated content, and AI systems retrain on the aggregate social information they influence. This interaction generates two feedback forces: an AI contagion channel, through which distortions diffuse across the network, and an AI social distortion multiplier, through which retraining amplifies past errors. Despite the high dimensionality of the environment, we show that the long-run behavior of the system admits a two-dimensional representation whose spectral radius determines whether AI-mediated information systems are dynamically stable or unstable. We characterize a sharp regulatory frontier identifying the minimum filtering required for stability and show how network topology shapes systemic informational risk.

title: The Generative Attributional Bond: Conceptual Foundations for a Generative Sociology

detail.title: The Generative Attributional Bond: Conceptual Foundations for a Generative Sociology
detail.abstract: Millions of people now sustain prolonged, emotionally significant, and cognitively formative exchanges with artificial systems whose ontological status remains undetermined. The available categories (use, interaction, relationship, parasocial relationship, prosthesis, assemblage) partially capture this phenomenon but fail to define its specific structure. This paper proposes the concept of the generative attributional bond to define this specific form of sustained coupling between a human and a responsive artificial entity. Its persistence depends on asymmetric reciprocal attributions, and it produces distributed cognitive, affective, linguistic, and sociotechnical transformations. The ontological question concerning the nature of the entity is methodologically suspended; what matters are the conditions under which attributions are sustained. In this paper, "generative" is used in a sociological rather than a computational sense: it refers to the transformative effects of the bond, not to the technical capacity of generative AI systems to produce outputs. On this basis, the paper proposes generative sociology as an emerging disciplinary field, organized through three analytical planes (epistemological, technological, and innovation), and three axes of development: research, training, and public engagement.

title: The Paradox of Trust: Why Cryptocurrency Supply Cannot Have a Global Upper Bound — On the “Scarcity/Verifiability/Non-Coerciveness” (SVN) Trilemma
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: The Paradox of Trust: Why Cryptocurrency Supply Cannot Have a Global Upper Bound — On the “Scarcity/Verifiability/Non-Coerciveness” (SVN) Trilemma

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests, employment relationships, consulting arrangements, funding sources, or other affiliations that could reasonably be perceived as influencing the conclusions of this work. This research was conducted independently.

detail.abstract:
This article argues that the total supply of cryptocurrencies cannot possess a meaningful global upper bound, not because of flaws in cryptographic algorithms themselves, but because of a structural contradiction between non-coerciveness, verifiability, and scarcity.

Starting from the trust problem that motivated Bitcoin, the article analyzes the necessary conditions for establishing universal trust in distributed systems. Following the insight of Ken Thompson's Reflections on Trusting Trust, it argues that any system claiming absolute credibility must remain fully transparent and verifiable across the entire execution chain, including source code, toolchains, deployment processes, and runtime behaviors.

From an engineering perspective, the article models the deployment of cryptocurrency systems as a process of parameter-bound instantiation. Once full verifiability is granted, the cost of creating communication-isolated variants approaches zero. Different communities, political groups, cultures, or economic interests may freely instantiate alternative but equally trustworthy systems, thereby continuously expanding the aggregate supply of equivalent resources.

The article then generalizes this observation into a trilemma theorem concerning distributed resourcegeneration systems: Scarcity (S), Verifiability (V), and Non-Coerciveness (N) cannot be simultaneously satisfied. A system that permits open verification without coercive exclusion cannot maintain globally enforceable scarcity.

Finally, the article argues that controlled inflation and externally imposed institutional constraints may represent not defects of civilization, but necessary mechanisms for resisting the natural concentration dynamics of purely mathematical systems.

title: Manufacturer-sponsored Digital Services Enhance Nanostore Competitiveness

detail.title: Manufacturer-sponsored Digital Services Enhance Nanostore Competitiveness
detail.abstract: Problem definition: Nanostores—small, independent grocery retailers serving Bottom-of-the-Pyramid consumers—constitute the largest retail channel in many developing countries, yet they increasingly face competition from convenience store chains that differentiate themselves through value-added digital services. Although such services can attract traffic and strengthen customer loyalty, most nanostores lack the financial and technological capabilities to invest in them independently. Because nanostores remain a strategically important channel for Consumer Packaged Goods manufacturers due to their scale and relatively high margins, manufacturers have begun supporting the digital transformation of these retailers. This paper investigates whether manufacturer-sponsored digital services effectively strengthen the competitiveness of the nanostore channel and increase manufacturers’ sales. Methodology/results: We collaborate with a large CPG manufacturer in Latin America that introduced a digital platform enabling nanostores to offer value-added services such as bill payments and mobile top-ups. Exploiting quasi-experimental variation and conducting econometric analyses that account for local retail competition, we examine whether adoption of the platform increases manufacturers’ sales to participating nanostores and whether any observed gains arise from cannibalization of neighboring stores. We find that adopting nanostores experience a significant increase in ordering volume, with evidence of cannibalization from nearby convenience stores over a very granular radius of 100 meters, but not from nearby nanostores. Overall, we find that value-added digital services organically expand total average sales within proximity retail channels, shifting market share to the more profitable nanostore channel. Managerial implications: Our findings suggest that manufacturer-sponsored digital services can organically expand the competitiveness and market share of the nanostore channel, generating benefits for both retailers and manufacturers. More broadly, the study highlights how CPG manufacturers in developing economies can strategically invest in retailer digitalization to strengthen traditional retail channels and sustain growth in underserved markets.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines a recurring governance condition across African continental integration architecture: the expansion of mobility rights for African nationals at a pace that exceeds the development of protection mechanisms available when those rights are exercised under conditions of political, economic, or social stress. The paper conceptualises this condition as the Continental Citizen Protection Deficit (CPD) and investigates its presence across five mobility corridors.


To assess variation in protection capacity, a Citizen Protection Deficit Index (CPDI Version 1.0) is proposed and applied provisionally to eight corridor pairs using transparent secondary-data indicators validated against independent institutional and peer-reviewed sources. Comparative analysis suggests that protection deficits are not isolated implementation failures but reflect recurring institutional design features observable across multiple mobility systems. Seven of eight assessed corridors were classified within the severity categories predicted by independent institutional evidence.


The paper identifies five architectural conditions associated with the emergence of the deficit and examines their implications for labour mobility, citizen protection and continental integration outcomes. A reform architecture grounded in existing African Union institutions is proposed and evaluated against political feasibility and implementation constraints. The paper concludes by specifying the conditions under which the CPD proposition would be falsified, thereby establishing clear boundaries for future empirical testing and framework refinement.

detail.abstract: This conceptual study advances a reframing of servant leadership by positioning it as a role construction mechanism that actively shapes followership within nonprofit organizations. Although existing research has largely emphasized a leader-centric perspective of the relationship between servant leadership and organizational or individual outcomes, substantially less attention has been directed toward the underlying processes through which leadership influences how followers interpret and enact their roles. To address this gap, the article integrates servant leadership theory, role theory, and followership theory to develop a cohesive conceptual framework that positions followership role orientation as a primary outcome. Within this framework, servant leadership is operationalized through relational, empowerment, and modeling practices that structure follower experiences within organizational contexts. These practices activate cognitive, psychological, and relational–affective mechanisms that shape how individuals interpret role expectations, construct role identities, and engage within leader–follower relationships. Through these mechanisms, followers develop role orientations that inform both how roles are understood and how they are enacted in practice. The framework adopts a process-oriented perspective that positions leadership as a defining force in the construction of organizational roles. By situating servant leadership within an interactive system of meaning-making and relational exchange, the model contributes to a more nuanced and theoretical understanding of leadership–followership dynamics in nonprofit organizations. Implications for theory and practice include advancing conceptual clarity, informing leadership development, and strengthening organizational effectiveness through the intentional cultivation of followership.

title: How Climate Shocks Produce Armed Rebellion: The 1970 Bhola Cyclone and the Birth of Bangladesh
affiliations: New Economic School (NES) and Yale School of Management

detail.title: How Climate Shocks Produce Armed Rebellion: The 1970 Bhola Cyclone and the Birth of Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
Why do climate shocks produce conflict (Hsiang et al., 2013)? We study the 1970 Bhola cyclone in East Pakistan, one of the deadliest natural disasters in recorded history, which killed an estimated 350,000 people. Using satellite imagery, archival records, electoral returns, and insurgent biographies, we show that cyclone exposure amplified pre-existing separatist sentiment at the ballot box and increased citizens’ subsequent participation in guerrilla warfare against the state. Our estimates imply that exposure to the cyclone’s devastation induced an additional 48,613 insurgents to join the guerrilla war effort. Effects are larger in areas with pre-existing political and economic grievances and weaker relief provision. Our analysis reveals the step-by-step mechanisms through which environmental shocks can produce conflict: they shift voting behavior, expose state indifference, and convert grievance into armed mobilization.

detail.abstract: While the experiential learning approach effectively improves financial literacy in developed countries, its applicability in developing countries faces resource constraints. However, expanding banking access in developing countries may enhance traditional financial education programs by enabling the practical application of learned financial concepts. Using a quasi-experimental design, we examine this hypothesis by evaluating the impact of Pakistan's flagship financial education program on the financial knowledge of primary school students and demonstrate that the program significantly improves students' financial knowledge. The literature assessing the effects of transportation infrastructure on how people and economic activity distribute themselves across a system of cities has three main parts. The theoretical literature makes robust predictions about how transportation infrastructure affects the internal structure of cities, but for systems of cities, theory does not let us rule much out. The city-level empirical literature establishes that improved urban transportation infrastructure causes suburban migration, but has only a small impact on city population. This literature is less helpful for understanding the effects of transportation infrastructure on the way people are distributed across a system of cities, but has made some progress. The small empirical literature looking at how transportation infrastructure affects systems of cities using cross-country data remains underdeveloped and is inconclusive.

detail.abstract: Fix a split-conformal calibration set and ask how often a fresh, independent draw from the score marginal falls under the threshold U (k). That realized coverage c = U (k) is a random variable; for independent calibration scores it follows the Beta(k, n-k + 1) law, variance about α(1-α)/n. We call this across-sample spread of realized coverage its dispersion, and the family of laws the dependence sweeps out the fan for short; we study how that dependence reshapes it. The organizing identity is that c is a functional of the count process alone, so its variance is governed by the count's covariance kernel, and negatively associated scores have a less variable count (Lemma 1). Three results follow. A leading-order fan coefficient: in a Bahadur regime Var(c) = n-2 Var(N (1-α)) + o(1/n), so the average pairwise covariance of the sub-threshold indicators sets the leading constant. An exact aggregate bound: summed over all levels k, negative association never widens the fan, by a convex-order contraction of the count against a concave functional and majorization. And, for equicorrelated normals, the single level is exact and monotone in the correlation, Var(Z (k)) = v k + ρ(1-v k), dispersively so via strong log-concavity and Tweedie's formula. We keep c (coverage against an independent test draw) distinct from conformal conditional coverage with an exchangeable test point: under dependence the mean of c is not pinned, and the positive-dependence decomposition we give is an exact identity that does not by itself order the fan against the independent one. The general single-level negative-association contraction is left as a conjecture, supported numerically. The governing sign is the one the companion note attaches to the finite de Finetti measure.

title: The Geometry and Dynamics of Power

detail.title: The Geometry and Dynamics of Power
detail.abstract: This study develops a statistical mechanics framework for nonequilibrium political dynamics by extending the Geometry of Power (Caesar Edward, 2025) to include porosity, vorticity, and viscosity as coupled fields within a multidimensional state space. Political regimes evolve along stochastic trajectories governed by path integrals, with dynamics driven by a free-action potential that combines the expected action, entropy, temperature, external pressure, and generalized political enthalpy. The framework adopts a coarse-grained macroscopic description in which microscopic political interactions are aggregated into effective ensemble observables that govern large-scale regime behavior. Porosity captures structural permeability and enables nonlocal transitions. Vorticity induces rotational dynamics and cyclical behavior, whereas viscosity introduces resistance and stabilizes trajectories. The resulting Langevin dynamics and associated Fokker–Planck equation describe the evolution of probability distributions over political states in the presence of turbulence. Empirical calibration using political and economic indicators, combined with a Monte Carlo simulation, generates trajectory ensembles from which entropy, generalized enthalpy, turbulence, and phase transitions are identified. When applied to East Africa, the framework reveals distinct dynamical regimes of stability, circulation, and confinement. The results demonstrate that political systems evolve through coupled stochastic processes rather than deterministic transitions, providing a unified basis for analyzing instability, structural burden, and long-term political change.

title: The Short- and Long-Run Effects of Railroads on Mexico-US Migration
affiliations: University of St Andrews and University of California, Davis - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Short- and Long-Run Effects of Railroads on Mexico-US Migration
detail.abstract:
This paper leverages variation in the access to the Mexican railroad network in the early 1900s to estimate its impact on migration to the United States and evaluate its long-run persistence after passenger rail service became obsolete. Using an IV strategy based on least-cost paths between historical cities, we find that locations with railroad access had migration rates four times higher than those without in the early twentieth century. Sequential migration was the key mechanism: railroads first facilitated internal mobility toward railroad hubs, then onward migration to the US. Railroad access also contributed to structural transformation, raising urbanization and local economic development. In terms of persistence, locations with historical railroad access show weakly lower total migration rates to the US in the early 21st century, consistent with local economic growth reducing the incentive to migrate. Yet destination-specific patterns prove remarkably durable: locations that disproportionately sent migrants to California, Arizona, or Texas in the 1900s continued to do so in the 2000s, reflecting the persistence of migrant networks.

detail.abstract: With the expansion of BRICS into BRICS+ in 2024, it has shown the potential for establishing a global order led by Global South countries. BRICs, officially launched in 2009 with four countries (China, Russia, India, Brazil), approved the accession of four new member countries (UAE, Egypt, Iran, Ethiopia) for the first time in 13 years since South Africa joined in 2011, and Indonesia formally joined as a member in 2025. Discussions are underway as to whether it will emerge as a new alternative to Western-centric economic cooperation, such as the G7, and the Bretton Woods financial order. (The rest omitted.)

title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Reliability and Scaling in Language Models
affiliations: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore

detail.title: Information-Theoretic Limits of Reliability and Scaling in Language Models

publicationDetails.journalName: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are evaluated as though perfect reliability is achievable for any task given sufficient scale. We show this assumption is information-theoretically unjustified. Every generative task has a reliability ceiling that no model can exceed, determined by how much output uncertainty is resolvable from observable context. The gap decomposes into a resolvable component closable with additional context and a subjective component inherent to task ambiguity. Autoregressive generation further degrades this ceiling at a rate governed by the task's dependency kernel, which quantifies inter-token correlations in the output. From these two primitives, we derive a first-principles scaling law where LLM performance is bottlenecked by the scarcer resource: training data or model capacity. This law recovers the Chinchilla scaling law as a special case and provides a structural account of when scaling improves reliability. Beyond scaling, our framework unifies diverse practical phenomena, such as the benefits of retrieval-augmentation and the spectral mechanics of catastrophic forgetting. Our work formalizes the resource-complexity tradeoffs that govern model performance across domains, offering a unified theory of performance limits in generative language models.

title: Do Wage Floors Increase Employment Risk for Workers with Disabilities? Evidence from Minimum Wage Increases and Subminimum Wage Repeal
affiliations: Stockton University,  and Rutgers University

detail.title: Do Wage Floors Increase Employment Risk for Workers with Disabilities? Evidence from Minimum Wage Increases and Subminimum Wage Repeal
detail.abstract:
People with disabilities are disproportionately represented in low-wage work, raising concerns that higher wage floors may reduce their employment opportunities, particularly for workers with more severe disabilities. We examine the effects of state minimum wage increases and state subminimum wage terminations on employment outcomes for people with disabilities using American Community Survey data from 2010–2023. We find little evidence that minimum wage increases reduce employment or labor force participation among people with disabilities, including those with more severe disabilities. While many estimates are statistically imprecise, confidence intervals generally rule out economically meaningful negative employment effects. We likewise find no evidence that terminating subminimum wages reduces employment opportunities for affected workers, and some estimates suggest positive employment effects for groups most likely to have been employed under subminimum wage arrangements. These gains may reflect complementary policies that often accompany repeal, such as Employment First initiatives. Overall, the results provide little support for the view that higher wage floors create disproportionate employment barriers for people with disabilities.

title: Place Marketing or Civic Information? Classifying Municipal Tweets using Machine Learning

detail.title: Place Marketing or Civic Information? Classifying Municipal Tweets using Machine Learning

declarations.funderStatement: Financial support from KEFU (Rådet för kommunalekonomisk forskning och utbildning) at Lund University School of Economics and Management is gratefully acknowledged.

publicationDetails.journalName: Research Institute of Industrial Economics (IFN) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: How do municipalities use social media? For place marketing, civic information, or dialogue with citizens? We address this question by classifying 35,930 tweets from 15 municipal Twitter accounts in the Skåne region of Sweden, using a machine learning algorithm trained on manually annotated data. Tweets are classified along two dimensions: whether they contain place marketing content and whether they contain civic information, yielding four categories. Our findings show that place marketing content declined substantially over the period studied, from nearly 40 percent of tweets in 2009 to just above 20 percent in 2018. In contrast, civic information and direct dialogue with citizens increased. These results suggest that the rise of social media has not trapped municipalities in a zero-sum place marketing arms race. Instead, municipalities appeared to be using Twitter increasingly as a channel for civic communication, with implications for how scholars and practitioners understand the evolving role of social media in place branding.

detail.abstract: This study’s core objective is to identify the direction and policy tasks for a new Northern Strategy amid the shifting global order. This report focuses its analysis on three fundamental aspects, striving to ensure consistency within its content. First, it comprehensively examines the new external environment and conditions for cooperation between South Korea and Northern countries in the era of global order restructuring in 2025. Second, it comprehensively evaluates the 35 years of Northern Policy implemented since the establishment of diplomatic relations with the Soviet Union in 1990, identifying key achievements, challenges, and future cooperation needs. Third, based on these new demands for cooperation, it analyzes the economic impact of the Northern Strategy. By synthesizing the results of this analysis, it proposes a new direction for the Northern Strategy and a plan for managing neighboring countries. (The rest omitted.)

title: Can You Judge without Doing? The Conditions for Decoupling Expertise in Evaluation from Production
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - NUS Business School and INSEAD

detail.title: Can You Judge without Doing? The Conditions for Decoupling Expertise in Evaluation from Production
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to produce knowledge work, a widespread worry is that human competence at evaluating the results could decline. For instance, if students never write code, the concern is that they will be unable to judge the code an AI writes for them. Yet evaluation without production is also routine: film critics judge cinematography without operating cameras, and wine critics rate vintages they could not make. We resolve this tension with a framework for analysing the Decoupling of Expertise in Evaluation and Production (DEEP), which specifies when production experience is necessary for competent evaluation and when it is not. We first separate two regimes of evaluation: in Regime 1, quality is fully determined by observable artefact features; in Regime 2, quality also depends on process attributes the finished artefact does not reveal. Next, we ask whether the information evaluators require in either regime can be acquired vicariously or only by producing. This framework predicts that the decline in human evaluative capabilities arising from cessation of production will be concentrated rather than universal. We also specify possible remedies by regime: training through simulation in Regime 1, process documentation in Regime 2, and modest quantities of production-for-calibration when these measures are infeasible.

detail.abstract: World Cup knockout matches are seeded using FIFA World Rankings, yet ELO ratings are widely regarded as a stronger alternative. This study examines which system better predicts knockout outcomes and whether FIFA’s 2018 shift to an ELO-inspired formula reduced the gap. Using 115 knockout matches from eight World Cups (1994–2022), we compared separate logistic regression models across six performance metrics. ELO outperformed FIFA on every measure, achieving higher prediction accuracy (73.9% vs. 68.7%), stronger discrimination (AUC 0.775 vs. 0.695), and better calibration (Brier score 0.189 vs. 0.220). FIFA’s 2018 reform improved performance and narrowed the accuracy gap from 6.0 to 3.2 percentage points, but did not eliminate it. Although McNemar’s test (p = 0.180) did not find a statistically significant accuracy difference, likely due to limited sample size, ELO exceeded FIFA in 89.8% of 10,000 bootstrap resamples and consistently outperformed across all evaluation metrics. Robustness checks confirmed that the advantage is structural rather than driven by data timing, specific tournaments, or ranking specifications.

title: Accountability Careers: Career Capital as Institutional Collateral in the AI Era

detail.title: Accountability Careers: Career Capital as Institutional Collateral in the AI Era

declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded

detail.abstract: This paper introduces and defends the term accountability careers as a distinctive, durable category of human work in the era of AI decision making. Accountability careers require the holder to have credentials, reputation or standing within the profession that amount to career capital that a rational person would seek to preserve. The career holder is vulnerable to sanctions and reputational damage which is a value proposition, not a weakness, given AI systems cannot have this attribute. The paper claims that this vulnerability is an asset that is the durable human function in an AI economy given that when consequential decisions go wrong institutions, courts, regulators and the public demand a named human with career capital that can be seized through public shame, professional license revocation, dismissal and criminal indictment. The argument proceeds by conceptual synthesis across moral psychology, procedural and interactional justice, AI governance, algorithmic management scholarship, and responsibility-gap philosophy. The construct is situated against Hochschild's emotional labor, the moral crumple zones described by Elish, Davies's accountability sinks, and Xing and Zheng's (2026) coinage of "accountability labor," which pertains to Chinese state surveillance. Accountability careers are differentiated from each. Four cases are evaluated from weakest to strongest: customer service chatbots (relatable with no real career capital), algorithmic hiring and firing (who is actually accountable in AI decisions), private sector healthcare AI and corporate disasters with named CEO accountability (the paradigm case, where the seizure of career capital (clawbacks, lifetime industry bans, criminal indictments) gives accountability its institutional bite). The close of the paper provides guidance on organizational design, AI governance, and career guidance with an emphasis on Gen Alpha, which is facing post-secondary decisions in the face of the rapid proliferation of AI in the job market.

title: The University Field - Why Reality Compels Interdisciplinarity and How Universities Must Respond
affiliations: University of Birmingham

detail.title: The University Field - Why Reality Compels Interdisciplinarity and How Universities Must Respond
detail.abstract: The modern university faces a contradiction that is simultaneously epistemological, institutional and historical. Reality increasingly presents itself through interconnected phenomena whose behaviour emerges from interactions among domains, while universities remain organised around disciplinary structures inherited from earlier centuries. These structures generated extraordinary advances in science, engineering, medicine, law and public administration. Yet the same structures now encounter growing difficulty when confronted with problems whose behaviour resides in relations rather than isolated components. This paper argues that interdisciplinarity is not a managerial aspiration or educational fashion. It is a compulsion imposed by reality upon the organisation of knowing. The paper traces the university from an earlier ideal of wholeness, through the Newtonian partition of knowledge into disciplines, to the fragmentation of the modern multiversity. It then examines how contemporary relational problems, including cities, climate change, infrastructure, public health, financial instability and artificial intelligence, expose the limits of disciplinary sovereignty. AI is treated not merely as another interdisciplinary topic but as a structural shock to the university's cognitive function, because it renders routine cognition increasingly available outside the university while pushing higher education back towards judgement, synthesis, trust, abstraction and foundational inquiry. The paper proposes the concept of the University Field, in which the university is understood as a field of inquiry, disciplines as nodes of depth and shared institutional capabilities as pools enabling movement across the field. The central claim is that the future university must preserve disciplinary depth while reorganising itself around the relational character of reality.

title: The Role of Shared Intention in the Effect of Social Value Orientation Similarity on Cooperative Behavior: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study
affiliations: Tianjin University of Technology and Education, Tianjin University of Technology and Education and Tianjin University of Technology and Education

detail.title: The Role of Shared Intention in the Effect of Social Value Orientation Similarity on Cooperative Behavior: An fNIRS Hyperscanning Study
detail.abstract: Cooperation is fundamental to human society, yet its success in social dilemmas depends not only on individual traits but also on the alignment of partners’ social preferences. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning, this study examined how similarity in social value orientation (SVO) influences cooperative behavior, shared intention, and inter-brain synchrony(IBS) during an iterated prisoner’s dilemma task.Behaviorally, homogeneous dyads (both pro-social or both pro-self) exhibited significantly higher and more stable cooperation rates than heterogeneous dyads, a relationship partially mediated by the formation of a shared intention. Neurally, we identified a neural synergy advantage effect in homophilic pairs, characterized by precise IBS in the right temporoparietal junction(rTPJ) alongside the strategic decoupling of the orbitofrontal cortex(OFC) and left inferior frontal gyrus(lIFG). Our work advances understanding of the mechanisms underlying cooperative heterogeneity and offers practical insights for optimizing team composition and collaboration in organizations.

title: From Lemons to Batteries: Information Frictions and Institutional Adaptation in Used-Car Markets

detail.title: From Lemons to Batteries: Information Frictions and Institutional Adaptation in Used-Car Markets
detail.abstract: This paper reviews information frictions in used-car markets and argues that their importance depends on the institutions that govern exchange. Mature internal-combustion-engine markets have not unraveled despite adverse selection because warranties, certified pre-owned programs, vehicle-history reports, dealer reputation, inspections, and disclosure rules have made many hidden-quality problems observable, certifiable, or insurable. The EV transition reopens this institutional problem. Battery health is central to used-EV value, range, depreciation, and warranty risk, but it is not well captured by mileage, age, title status, or accident history. Because battery condition is difficult for buyers to verify and compare, used-EV markets require new institutions for battery-health disclosure, certification, warranties, and data portability. The central lesson is that used-car market efficiency is not automatic; it is an institutional achievement that must be rebuilt as vehicle technology changes.

title: CDSCO Guidance on Medical Device Software: A Study On the Evolving Definition of SaMD versus SiMD

detail.title: CDSCO Guidance on Medical Device Software: A Study On the Evolving Definition of SaMD versus SiMD
detail.abstract: The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) issued its Draft Guidance Document on Medical Device Software on October 21, 2025. The document draws a formal distinction between Software in a Medical Device (SiMD) and Software as a Medical Device (SaMD), a distinction that has been quietly building in regulatory practice for several years but never squarely addressed in Indian law. This paper examines how that distinction has evolved, what the draft guidance actually says about each category, and whether the document changes anything of substance or merely describes the existing framework in clearer language. The short answer, at least for now, is that it does the latter. But the implications of describing things clearly are not trivial, and the paper argues that the guidance, if implemented carefully, could meaningfully reduce the compliance burden on software developers while protecting patients.

title: The PBM Gross-to-Net Fallacy and the Emerging IRA/MFN Pricing Environment

detail.title: The PBM Gross-to-Net Fallacy and the Emerging IRA/MFN Pricing Environment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

contentType.other: Working Draft of Research Project as a Paper

detail.abstract:
Background. U.S. branded drug list prices,  Wholesale Acquisition Costs (WAC), anchor every downstream reimbursement formula, yet match the transaction price for essentially no payer. The gap between list and net revenue, the "gross-to-net bubble," reached an estimated $356 billion for brand drugs in 2024. This review asks how manufacturers build the WAC, why it systematically overstates the realized Average Sales Price (ASP), and how the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) and the 2025 Most-Favored-Nation (MFN) executive order alter that logic

Methods. Because realized net prices and rebate splits reside in confidential commercial contracts and cannot be pooled, the study is a gray-literature review using structured narrative synthesis rather than meta-analysis. This effort involved screening and selecting sources following a PRISMA-informed process and tiered by reliability: Tier 1 primary government and legal records, Tier 2 peer-reviewed methodology and policy journals, and Tier 3 trade institutes and consultancies. Each cited claim traces to a digital object identifier (DOI), PubMed identifier (PMID), or official URL. The analysis traces one artifact, the WAC, across construction, divergence, and policy compression.

Results. Manufacturers construct the WAC through five frameworks. These include analog benchmarking, quality-adjusted life year (QALY) value modeling, willingness-to-pay research, discounted-cash-flow recovery, and strategic rebate-room engineering. These function not as independent checks but as a rationalization stack producing the maximum defensible price. The resulting list-to-net divergence is structurally inevitable. Five forces (the Medicaid best-price trap, escalating rebate walls, 340B volume growth, the IRA Part D manufacturer discount, and access barriers) drive realized ASP to 40–60% of WAC, and below in highly rebated classes. Patients pay cost-sharing on the inflated anchor while intermediaries capture the rebate. First-round Medicare negotiation cut prices 38–79% below the list. The MFN order anchors U.S. prices to the lowest gross domestic product (GDP)-adjusted price among comparable nations, dismantling each pillar of the construction architecture.

Conclusions. The gross-to-net gap is not market inefficiency. Instead, it represents a system operating as designed, with the list price serving as an instrument for rebate generation. The IRA and MFN compress the headroom on which that logic depends. However, patients benefit only if WAC actually falls and cost-sharing is redesigned on the net price. The structural transformation is real. Its distribution is not yet determined. The review contributes 1) a unified causal account linking list-price construction, the rebate economy, and the 2022–2026 policy rupture; 2) a tiered, verifiability-governed gray-literature method for a domain whose decisive data are confidential; and 3) a literature-to-question mapping that makes the evidence base for each research question explicit and auditable.
