detail.abstract:
This paper generalizes the mechanism of False Cognitive Power Transfer (FCPT) into a unified theory of cognitive autonomy loss (FCPT-G) applicable across human, social, institutional, and artificial systems. FCPT-G is defined as the process by which a cognitive or semi-cognitive system erroneously attributes to its own autonomy a capacity that is in fact generated, partially or wholly, by an external source.

The paper distinguishes this pathological misattribution from functional cognitive offloading and develops a phenomenological model of autonomy degradation, including a formulation of the accumulated cognitive deficit as the integrated area between a critically sustained trajectory and an uncritically eroded one.

The model's exponential form is grounded in the established skill-decay literature (Ebbinghaus; Arthur et al., 1998), and its core phenomena are supported by recent empirical findings (Shen & Tamkin, 2026; Kosmyna et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026; Qian & Wexler, 2024; Perry et al., 2023).

The framework yields testable predictions at individual, social, and systemic levels, integrates with the Maslow7F coherence model and Information Gravity Theory (IGT-G), and proposes ROGO, ERGO EMERGO as an active recovery mechanism. The paper carries practical implications for education, AI governance, and the design of human-AI systems that preserve rather than erode cognitive sovereignty.

title: Exploring New Angles Of Reality In Chinua Achebes Anthills Of The Savannah
affiliations: Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, Students

detail.title: Exploring New Angles Of Reality In Chinua Achebes Anthills Of The Savannah
detail.abstract: Language has is a powerful tool for the work of literature. The language of ambiguity which literature adopts has given the universe of discourse the opportunity and the ability to explore and to think beyond the past. And the process of repetition of what has been in existence by digging deeper into the body of the text in deciding what will count as truth by uncovering the buried truth in a literary text. This is because one unravels the meaning of a text through the use of language. Language is, therefore, subject to uncertainties; It is a resistant tool that determines or fixes meanings. This article examines this claim as a footnote, In other words, the methods by which the truth has been rebuilt and reimagined, and the manner in which imitation exposes the claim that, almost the same but not quite, made by Said and Bhabha (1994). This study uses textual analysis to examine by Chinua Achebe's Anthills of Savannah through the lens of postcolonial theory, trying to figure out what propelled the characters to imitate one other in rebuilding reality. Also to investigates the possible ways in which the characters engaged in mimicry and reconstruction of truth in the selected novel.

title: Information, Externalities, and the Limits of the Market: A Shannon-Theoretic Reading of the Coase Theorem

detail.title: Information, Externalities, and the Limits of the Market: A Shannon-Theoretic Reading of the Coase Theorem

This article is a theoretical contribution and uses no primary data.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a formal correspondence between Shannon's mathematical theory of communication and Coase's theorem on social cost. By interpreting the vendor as a sender, the buyer as a receiver, the transaction as transmitted information, and externalities as channel noise, we argue that the Coase theorem can be recovered as a limiting case of the Noisy Channel Coding Theorem, obtained when channel capacity is unbounded. The mapping yields two observable consequences. First, property rights operate as channel codes whose redundancy structure determines how efficiently externalities are internalized; this predicts that markets with finer-grained rights (individual transferable quotas, registered water rights, contractually specified ecosystem-service flows) should exhibit lower and less persistent externalities than markets where the same physical good is described by a coarser code. Second, transaction costs determine an upper bound on the volume of welfare-relevant exchanges a market can sustain (a market analogue of channel capacity) beyond which no institutional refinement can keep externalities internalized, predicting threshold behavior in environmental markets at high volumes of activity. The framework recasts the Pigou-Coase debate as a choice between modifying the source distribution and modifying the channel code and offers a candidate metric for institutional quality (the market entropy) that, unlike most welfare measures in environmental economics, is in principle estimable from data on intended and realized transactions.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence adoption does not merely flatten the Phillips Curve-it transforms its geometry across four distinct technological regimes. We develop a dual- channel production framework: AI acts as a total factor productivity shifter A(θt) = A0eλTFPθt and a direct factor substitute with regime-contingent elasticity σ2(θt). The TFP channel produces level shifts; the substitution channel produces geometric transformation-including an axis inversion in Regime III where inflation causes unemployment rather than the reverse. The Phillips Curve is derived as a theorem from first principles. We prove that Regimes I and II are not separable from standard indicators (πt,ut): the KL divergence between their emission distributions is bounded regardless of sample size. A regime-contingent policy framework and six falsifiable empirical predictions are provided. The geometric intuition was developed by the author in 2016.

title: Why Sustainable Brands Can't Scale in India: Diagnosing the Intent-Action Gap in Ethical Consumption

detail.title: Why Sustainable Brands Can't Scale in India: Diagnosing the Intent-Action Gap in Ethical Consumption

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest. No financial or personal relationships with any organization could be perceived to have influenced this research.

detail.abstract:
India's sustainable consumer goods market exhibits a persistent paradox: urban consumers report high purchase intent toward eco-friendly and organic products, yet the category holds under 2% of FMCG market share, and its leading D2C brands operate at thin or negative margins. This study investigates why this intention-action gap resists structural closure among urban Indian consumers within India's phygital retail environment.

Using a structured primary survey (n = 112, Mumbai Metropolitan Region, February 2026) across 14 items, the study quantifies a mean intent-action gap of 1.81 points on a continuous 10-point scale, with 80.4% of respondents purchasing sustainably less often than they intend to.

Applying a thirteen-framework diagnostic architecture spanning consumer behaviour, behavioural economics, market structure theory, and business model design, the study identifies six interlocking structural mechanisms: a unit economics deadlock, a greenwashing-sustained trust failure structured as a Prisoner's Dilemma, a phygital distribution mismatch, a definitional divergence between consumer and brand framings of sustainability, the credence good structure of the category, and the self-reinforcing interaction of these barriers across three structural loops.

The study's original contribution is the empirical demonstration that these barriers are mutually sustaining, and that no single lever commands a majority, because each remaining barrier absorbs any partial fix. A synthesis in Section 5.9 identifies the verification gap, defined as the constitutional inability to confirm a credence good's core benefit through use alone, as the root structural condition from which all six barriers derive their persistence. Seven directional recommendations and a minimum viable intervention bundle (R1, R3, R4) are derived for mid-scale sustainable D2C brands, operationally feasible without requiring breakthrough cost reduction or VC-scale capital investment.

title: The Phenomenon of Freed Prisoners in the Arab Republic of Egypt: Between Humanitarian Dimensions, Policy Deviations, and Determinants of Public Security and the Rule of Law

detail.title: The Phenomenon of Freed Prisoners in the Arab Republic of Egypt: Between Humanitarian Dimensions, Policy Deviations, and Determinants of Public Security and the Rule of Law

keywords: FEDA (Functional and Engineering Dissection Analysis) Governing Philosophy: Positive Neutrality & Sovereign Resilience Liberated Prisoners

detail.abstract: This study addresses, through sociological and policy analysis, the phenomenon of liberated Palestinian prisoners residing in the Arab Republic of Egypt, within the context of post-conflict environments and the humanitarian repositioning emerging from the events in the Gaza Strip. By applying the "Functional and Engineering Dissection Analysis" (FEDA) methodology, the paper deconstructs the socio-psychological dimensions formed within Zionist isolation ("cell psychology") and the resulting behavioral symptoms, such as the mentality of absolute entitlement and the authority complex. The study also monitors the growing sociological gap between the factional privileges granted to freed prisoners and the reality of the displaced popular incubator, which has spontaneously aligned with the "legitimacy of direct pain" at the expense of protocol-driven symbols. The paper highlights the procedural deviations of the factions and the risks of external ideological dependency on regional axes, demonstrating how this behavior transformed into a direct infringement on public policies, diplomatic norms, and public security and order in the host state. The study concludes by offering firm strategic determinants and recommendations, emphasizing the necessity of a critical review of the "prisoner-leader" concept and subjecting all activities and blocs to the rule of law and public order.

title: Platform-Controlled Search and Distortions in Attention Allocation
affiliations: Peking University - HSBC School of Business,  and University of Toronto - Department of Economics

detail.title: Platform-Controlled Search and Distortions in Attention Allocation
detail.abstract: We study a monopoly platform that sets meeting rates between buyers and two seller types: niche sellers, whose higher-quality good appeals to only some buyers, and mass-market sellers, whose good appeals to all. Sellers compete by posting prices à la Burdett and Judd (1983), so buyer surplus requires competition, while platform revenue requires seller rents. This tension creates a systematic distortion: as search capacity grows, the platform keeps niche exposure just past the saturation point---where extra attention erodes rents---and diverts the rest to mass-market sellers. Applied to Amazon product search and Google passage-ranking data, the model indicates buyer-surplus losses of 63 and 44 percent of the planner's benchmark, respectively. Letting buyer participation respond to the platform's recommendations disciplines it and shrinks this loss.

title: Local Labor Market Tightness and Job Quality: Evidence from Job Changers
affiliations: W.E. Upjohn Institute for Employment Research, U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) - Economic Research Service (ERS), Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Local Labor Market Tightness and Job Quality: Evidence from Job Changers
detail.abstract: We examine how labor market tightness affects workers' job amenities and quality. Using novel data from the Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking (SHED), and multiple measures of labor market tightness, we estimate that a 10 percent increase in job vacancies per thousand residents leads to a 7-12 percent increase in the probability of changing jobs, an 11-18 percent increase in the (unconditional) probability of switching to a self-assessed overall better job, and similar-size increases in pay and benefits, interest in the work, and better opportunities for advancement. Tight labor markets thus not only improve worker pay, in line with earlier studies, but also improve job amenities more broadly, and by roughly the same proportion. Consequently, the benefits to workers of a tight labor market are likely underestimated when based on pay alone.

title: Refineries, Pipelines and Petroleum Fields - The Impact of Oil on Conflict Around the World

detail.title: Refineries, Pipelines and Petroleum Fields - The Impact of Oil on Conflict Around the World
detail.abstract: We study how global oil price shocks affect the spatial distribution of violent conflict. Combining monthly georeferenced data on oil infrastructure with conflict events worldwide over 1989-2021, we exploit exogenous variation in world crude oil prices within countries using grid-cell and country*month fixed effects. Oil price increases raise organized conflict in oil-bearing cells but reduce it in nearby non-oil areas, indicating a spatial reallocation of territorial violence toward economically valuable locations rather than a uniform increase in conflict. By contrast, lower-intensity unrest spreads across neighboring cells, consistent with diffuse grievance and mobilization channels. The effect is strongest for petroleum fields and driven by state-based conflict, consistent with intensified contestation over oil rents, while downstream infrastructure is associated with protests and localized violence. The magnitude of the response varies with ethnic exclusion, institutions, geography, and ownership, pointing to rent-contestation mechanisms shaped by local conditions.
